noticias.titulo: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
noticias.resumen: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
- Published
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (Â£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.
"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.
"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

noticias.titulo: Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
noticias.resumen: Markle is being held in custody in the US after one charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.
noticias.texto:
Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
- Published
Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.
Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.
Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

noticias.titulo: Russian military plane crashes, killing all 19 on board
noticias.resumen: Russia's defence ministry says it preliminarily believes a technical malfunction was the cause of the crash in the Kemerovo region.
noticias.texto:
Russian military plane crashes, killing all 19 on board
- Published
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

noticias.titulo: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
noticias.resumen: The Metropolitan Police say he has been taken into custody by the US Military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.
noticias.texto:
American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
- Published
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

noticias.titulo: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
noticias.resumen: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.
noticias.texto:
William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive Â£1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.
Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.
Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.
During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.
Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.
Earthshot Prize 2026 - full list of winners
- Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land
- Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
- Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters
- Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
- Fix Our Climate: Ãrsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind
The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.
Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.
As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.
The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.
Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.
As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."
The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.

noticias.titulo: Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit
noticias.resumen: The Prince and Princess of Wales are visiting Mumbai for the Earthshot Prize this week, but started their trip with some fun outings.
noticias.texto:
Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit
The Prince and Princess of Wales have played street cricket and taken a trip on the metro during the first day of their three-day visit to India.
In the coming days, the royal couple will be attending events for the Earthshot Prize, which William founded, as well as meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
It marks the first time in four years that William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together - following Catherine's treatment for cancer.
The BBC's senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph explains more.

noticias.titulo: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
noticias.resumen: Rescuers found the pet cat in the ruins of Zariah's apartment four days after she made an emotional plea to the public.
noticias.texto:
Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.
Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.
City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.
Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
noticias.resumen: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
noticias.texto:
As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
- Published
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

noticias.titulo: Who to watch in Spain's election race
noticias.resumen: Spain votes on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule.
noticias.texto:
Who to watch in Spain's election race
- Published
Spanish voters face a snap election on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule under Pedro SÃ¡nchez.
The left had hoped to focus on Spain's housing crisis, but the government has been buffeted by corruption scandals, a migrant crisis, and most recently rail disasters that left 115 people dead. Here are the key figures to look out for in the race to run Spain's next government.
Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o (People's Party)
FeijÃ³o's People's Party (PP) tops most of the polls and as leader of the conservative opposition since 2022 he is favourite to become Spain's next prime minister.
His pitch to voters is his experience and reputation as a capable administrator, with 13 years as president of the north-west Galicia region from 2009.
"It's called management: and it's what I know how to do, it's what I want to do, and it's the change Spain needs," he has told voters.
FeijÃ³o has held public office continuously since 1991, and although he guided the PP to win the biggest number of seats in parliament in 2023, they fell short of an outright parliamentary majority. SÃ¡nchez's Socialist PSOE stayed in power through deals with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and pro-independence groups.
FeijÃ³o says the best outcome for Spain would be a PP majority governing alone, with support in parliament from far-right party Vox. His party has worked in coalition with Vox in four Spanish regions, and he has not ruled out a national coalition under strict conditions and red lines.
Unlike SÃ¡nchez, the PP leader is not well known internationally and his lack of English may hold him back on the world stage. FeijÃ³o admits to making little effort to learn English but believes the "enormous problems" faced by Spaniards are of greater importance: "I don't know English, but I know how to govern."
Pedro SÃ¡nchez (Socialists)
SÃ¡nchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.
He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.
SÃ¡nchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.
But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.
The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.
He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.
JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, who was transport minister in SÃ¡nchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos CerdÃ¡n awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
SÃ¡nchez's wife, BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David SÃ¡nchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.
In a defiant message, BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".
- Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election 
  - Published5 October
- Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike 
  - Published6 days ago
Santiago Abascal (Vox)
SÃ¡nchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.
Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.
Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro SÃ¡nchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.
He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".
The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.
His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.
He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.
Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.
Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.
Ada Colau (The Broad Front)
Former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Frente Amplio (Broad Front) - which has lost many of its supporters in recent weeks to the Socialists and is currently polling in fourth place.
Previously called Sumar, the coalition was in government with the Socialists under leader Yolanda DÃaz, but she decided she would not run again. Colau came into politics as a housing activist and fair rents and housing is one of her coalition's big policies.
Other parties on the left are contesting the election separately, including the pro-Catalan independence Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC) under Gabriel RufiÃ¡n who has reached a campaign deal with Podemos under Irene Montero.
- Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies 
  - Published8 October
MÃriam Nogueras (Junts)
Catalan centre-right pro-independence party Junts per Catalunya played a pivotal role in supporting Pedro SÃ¡nchez's government, even though it had just seven seats in the 350-seat Congress, and it may be central to post-election negotiations too. It was Junts' decision to reject the government's housing proposals last month that pushed the Socialist leader into snap elections.
Its lead candidate is MÃriam Nogueras, who has made clear that Catalan demands come first for her party. Junts president Carles Puigdemont, 63, is planning to return to Spain after the election. He has lived in self-imposed exile since 2017 after leading Catalonia's failed bid for independence.
Other key figures to watch
Isabel DÃaz Ayuso, 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.
Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.
Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.
Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.
Socialist Carlos Cuerpo, 46, was chosen by Pedro SÃ¡nchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.
He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".
In the same light, SÃ¡nchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have FeijÃ³o and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."
Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed SÃ¡nchez to remain as leader.
Carlos HernÃ¡ndez Quero, 30, has been a Vox MP since 2023, and speaks for the party on housing and urban affairs, taking charge of one of the most important election issues.
He is not regarded as the party's second-in-command, a position more commonly associated with figures such as Montserrat LluÃs or Ignacio Garriga, but he is media-savvy and known for his clear, combative defence of Vox's economic policies and proposals.
Further to the right is Alvise PÃ©rez, 36, a Member of the European Parliament who leads Se AcabÃ³ la Fiesta (The party is over). His party won three seats in European elections in 2024 and attracts voters disappointed with Vox. His party adopts a hard line on immigration, corruption and the EU.

noticias.titulo: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
noticias.resumen: Illegal activities in the Amazon pose grave risks to uncontacted Indigenous groups like Brazil’s Awa,.
noticias.texto:
Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
Illegal activities in the Amazon pose grave risks to uncontacted Indigenous groups like Brazil’s Awa, advocates stress.
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
Pressure on the forest
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups, mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

noticias.titulo: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
noticias.resumen: US president expected to meet with Chinese leader for third time this year; hold trilateral summit with Putin.
noticias.texto:
What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
US president expected to meet with Chinese leader for third time this year; possible trilateral summit with Putin.
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.
The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.
Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.
The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.
“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.
As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.
Progress on AI?
Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.
As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.
In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.
Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.
Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.
“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”
The Nvidia scandal
The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.
Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.
“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.
Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.
Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.
The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.
China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.
Taiwan
Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.
Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.
The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.
In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.
The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.
“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.
For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.
Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.
“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.
Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.
Trade breakthroughs?
US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.
By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent, while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.
Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.
A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.
“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”
US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.
Those purchases have also lagged behind the commitments.
A Putin-Xi-Trump meeting
The most significant outcome of this year’s APEC summit may be the three-way meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.
Such a meeting would likely be seen as a massive boon for Putin.
“By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognised as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah,” Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution, wrote in a recent analysis.
Xi, in turn, would “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other”.
The benefit for Trump, who the White House says will focus on denuclearisation efforts, remains less clear, according to experts.
“A trilateral meeting would showcase the extent to which both Trump and Putin seek to curry favour with Xi,” Crisis Group’s Wyne said.
“It would also further unnerve US allies and partners that fear Trump’s openness to an informal ‘G2’ or ‘G3’ arrangement,” he said, referring to a global realignment that bypasses other world powers.

noticias.titulo: Prosecutors allege man ‘destroyed’ US military plane at Irish airport
noticias.resumen: Daithi O'Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight.
noticias.texto:
Prosecutors allege man ‘destroyed’ US military plane at Irish airport
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight.
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
Smashed every gauge in the cockpit
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.
According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.
He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit.
O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks.
“As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.
“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.”
Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

noticias.titulo: Man charged over ‘brutal attack’ on Somali-American in Minnesota
noticias.resumen: Rideshare driver Mohamed Yusuf is in a critical condition after he was allegedly assaulted by a passenger.
noticias.texto:
Man charged over ‘brutal attack’ on Somali-American in Minnesota
Rideshare driver Mohamed Yusuf is in a critical condition after he was allegedly assaulted by a passenger.
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.
Mohamed Yusuf, 51, suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma.
“It was an incredibly brutal attack,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Tuesday.
She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday.
Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation.
Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said.
The court filing said Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1am on Saturday. His brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like the name Mohamed.
“He was apparently pulled out of the car and was standing there when Patel drove over him and might have circled back and driven over him again,” Moriarty said.
Uber ‘horrified’
Patel’s parents called police for a wellness check after he arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior”, according to the court filing.
When the officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was”, the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, that it has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
Rights advocates have raised concerns about rhetoric against Somali Americans by US President Donald Trump and his allies, and condemned his immigration crackdown in Minnesota.
US rights advocates have also noted rising Islamophobia over the past two-plus decades following the September 11, 2001, attacks, and more recently due to anti-immigration policies, rising white supremacy movements and the fallout from Israel’s war on Gaza.

noticias.titulo: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
noticias.resumen: The US-led board has decried continued fighting in Gaza and delays in implementing the terms of a 2025 ceasefire deal.
noticias.texto:
Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
The US-led board has decried continued fighting in Gaza and delays in implementing the terms of a 2025 ceasefire deal.
The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza.
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained.
The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza.
Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
‘Cannot be sustained indefinitely’
In recent weeks, Israel has continued to carry out deadly air strikes, and its ongoing restrictions have prevented the delivery of life-saving aid into Gaza ahead of the winter season.
“Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the board said in its report.
According to the board, the widespread devastation in Gaza has left Palestinians facing “another winter in tents and rubble”.
Trump first proposed the Board of Peace in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
The board’s mission was laid out in a 20-point Gaza peace plan, as well as the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire formally began on October 10, 2025, though attacks have continued since.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
But in Tuesday’s report, the board said Israel and Hamas have fallen far short of their commitments in the ceasefire deal.
“A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”
The board also noted that Israel has blocked the technocratic civil administration body created to run Gaza on an interim basis.
“The absence of decisions by the government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan,” the report said.
“The Board of Peace calls on the government of Israel to take these decisions without delay.”
To break the deadlock, the board called on the UN Security Council to press both sides to fulfil their agreements.
“Neither party may treat the other’s delay as license for its own inaction, and together these obligations are the only route to Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction at scale,” the report said.
It also added that the outcome must establish a credible path towards Palestinian statehood and self-determination, warning that no unilateral actions should be permitted to derail that ultimate goal.

noticias.titulo: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
noticias.resumen: Crew say their boat was attacked by drones launched from US-operated vessel as part of 'manifestly unlawful' campaign.
noticias.texto:
Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
Crew says their boat was attacked by drones launched from US-operated vessel as part of ‘manifestly unlawful’ campaign.
A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March.
The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just.
It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador.
“We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.”
The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months.
A report from the Washington Post in August, however, suggested that the vessels were targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission.
Other reports have raised the possibility of the attacks being conducted by a US government contractor or a regional ally.
The attacks appear to be similar to an ongoing campaign the US military has claimed credit for.
Since September 2025, the US government has publicly undertaken a series of boat strikes, with the aim of killing alleged “narcoterrorists”.
At least 244 people have been killed as part of that campaign, which experts have described as extrajudicial killing, in violation of international law.
The lawsuit filed on Monday alleges that two drones were launched from a vessel operated by the US in March and proceeded to attack La Negra Francisca Duarte II.
The boat was set ablaze, resulting in “serious burns” for two of the 16 crew members.
“All of the Plaintiffs ended up jumping off the ship and into the sea. They then found their way onto small emergency boats,” the filing said, calling the strike part of an “unprecedented and manifestly unlawful US military campaign”.
After the strike, the crew members say they made their way towards what they believed was a tuna fishing boat nearby but were met by armed men speaking English dressed in military uniforms.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he has launched a hardline campaign to combat drug trafficking into the US.
That push has coincided with a policy of expanding US military operations across Latin America, often in collaboration with right-wing political allies in the region.
But critics have raised concerns over transparency and potential rights abuses during such operations.
No suspects have been identified in the boat strike campaign undertaken by the US military, for instance, nor has any evidence been presented to the public.
Families, however, have stepped forward to claim the dead as their loved ones. Many have argued that the people killed in the boat strike campaign were not drug traffickers but fishermen and informal workers.
In December 2025, the family of the missing Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza filed a complaint about the boat strikes through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, claiming his right to life had been violated.
A few weeks later, in January, the families of two workers from Trinidad and Tobago – Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo – filed a wrongful death lawsuit in a US federal court in Massachusetts. The men had reportedly been travelling home from Venezuela after taking work abroad.
But experts say that efforts to hold the US government to account will be difficult, given the lack of transparency surrounding the boat strikes.
The lethal boat strike campaign has continued in recent weeks, with a recent attack taking place on October 27.
The US government has also been involved in non-lethal interception efforts, stopping suspected drug-trafficking boats.
The watchdog group Human Rights Watch said that the US and Ecuador intercepted at least eight vessels between late August and mid-September, on the basis that they were being used to supply drug trafficking groups.
Of the 160 crew members on board those vessels, Human Rights Watch says that 56 were released without charge by court order, 40 were acquitted for lack of evidence, 50 are awaiting trial, and 14 were not formally charged.

noticias.titulo: DR Congo’s rival peace efforts fail to halt violence in the east
noticias.resumen: Diplomatic efforts struggle to end fighting in eastern DRC as civilians continue to bear the cost of conflict.
noticias.texto:
DR Congo’s rival peace efforts fail to halt violence in the east
Diplomatic efforts struggle to end fighting in eastern DRC as civilians continue to bear the cost of conflict.
Bukavu, DRC – For residents of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the succession of diplomatic initiatives meant to end years of conflict is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the violence unfolding around them.
In North and South Kivu provinces, fighting between the Congolese army and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), an armed and political coalition led by former President Joseph Kabila, has continued despite international efforts to secure a settlement. Civilians remain exposed to attacks, displacement and the disruption of essential services.
The latest escalation has raised questions about whether negotiations in Washington and Doha can deliver security on the ground, and whether the separate diplomatic efforts are sufficiently coordinated to make progress.
“One meeting follows another, and they all end up being much the same,” said Blaise Chasumba, a resident of Bukavu, the provincial capital of South Kivu. “But the real peace that the warring parties are dangling before us is far from becoming a reality on the ground. We continue to lose our loved ones and our homes.”
A conflict with deep historical roots
The Washington Accords, signed in December 2025, seek to address tensions between the DRC and neighbouring Rwanda. The Doha process, by contrast, is intended to resolve the conflict between the Congolese government and the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which includes the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group.
The distinction is important: an agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali cannot, on its own, resolve the confrontation between the Congolese government and armed groups operating inside the country.
The Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed by the DRC government, the AFC and M23 on November 15, 2025. In August 2026, representatives of the two sides, alongside Qatar, the United States, Togo, the African Union Commission and Switzerland, agreed on a road map to advance negotiations and establish a mechanism to review implementation. Fighting has nevertheless continued.
The roots of the conflict stretch back decades. The 1994 genocide in neighbouring Rwanda and the flight of former Rwandan soldiers and militia members into what was then Zaire helped create the conditions for successive wars. The presence of armed groups linked to the genocide, and the emergence of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), became a persistent source of tension between Kinshasa and Kigali.
The First and Second Congo Wars, which began in 1996 and 1998, drew in several neighbouring countries. Although the conflicts formally ended, disputes over land, political representation, citizenship and control of natural resources continued to drive violence in the east.
M23 emerged in 2012 after a mutiny by former members of the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP). The group had been integrated into the Congolese army under a March 23, 2009 peace agreement, which its leaders later accused the government of failing to honour. The United Nations and conflict researchers have documented the movement’s origins in the breakdown of that integration process.
The diplomatic landscape has since become more complicated. Established in October 2026 under Kabila’s leadership, the FRN says it has succeeded the AFC and assumed its commitments. The precise relationship between the new coalition and the earlier AFC/M23 structure remains important when assessing who is represented in the negotiations.
On the battlefield, an offensive in early November underlined the fragility of the diplomatic process. FRN fighters advanced through Kahuzi-Biega National Park and along National Road 3, a strategic route linking Bukavu with areas farther north.
Conflict monitoring reports said the fighters captured several localities, including Bitale and the centre of Bulambika on November 8 . The Congolese army said it had halted the advance at Bulambika and was preparing a counteroffensive. Local and military accounts differed over the extent of the fighters’ territorial gains.
Diplomatic commitments, limited progress
The fighting has driven further displacement and placed additional pressure on communities already struggling with years of conflict. Humanitarian organisations have warned that conflict is also making it harder to maintain essential services.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said it had reduced its staff presence in the Bunyakiri health zone, relocating some personnel to Bitale and Bukavu as the security situation deteriorated.
“We remind all parties to the conflict of the importance and the obligation to respect and ensure the protection of healthcare facilities, civilian populations and humanitarian staff, in accordance with international humanitarian law,” MSF said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera.
The Congolese armed forces, known by their French acronym FARDC, have blamed recent attacks in North and South Kivu on the Rwandan army and fighters allied with the FRN. The army says it is preparing operations to recover lost positions.
Rwanda denies supporting armed groups in eastern DRC, citing the presence of the FDLR as a security threat. The dispute has remained central to tensions between the two countries.
In a resolution adopted in February 2025, the UN Security Council condemned M23’s offensive and described direct support and participation by the Rwanda Defence Force. It called on Rwanda to end its support and withdraw its forces from Congolese territory. The resolution also condemned support provided by Congolese forces to armed groups, particularly the FDLR, and called for the group’s neutralisation.
The African Union (AU) has acknowledged the gap between diplomatic commitments and conditions on the ground. In a communique issued after a Peace and Security Council meeting on October 26 , it said implementation of commitments under the Washington and Doha processes remained limited. It called for better coordination between the initiatives and urged inclusive, nationally owned dialogue.
The AU’s assessment points to a central weakness in the peace efforts: Agreements and diplomatic meetings have not translated into a sustained improvement in security. The bloc has stressed that a lasting settlement requires political dialogue involving wider sections of Congolese society, including women, young people and civil society organisations.
Civilians demand a voice in the peace process
For some Congolese, negotiations between governments and armed groups are not enough. They want a broader political process that addresses the grievances sustaining the conflict.
Dieumerci Mungu Akonkwa, North Kivu coordinator for Action for Democracy and Development in the Congo, said the negotiations had yet to produce tangible improvements for civilians.
“Since these negotiations began on the ground, there has been no progress. All that is happening is that the lives of peaceful civilians are being cut short. The war continues to create displaced people, and women are being raped,” he said.
Akonkwa called for an inclusive national dialogue, pointing to proposals put forward by Catholic and Protestant church leaders. Such a process, he argued, could bring political actors and civil society into discussions that extend beyond negotiations between the government and armed groups.
The challenge is not only to secure commitments from the parties to the conflict, but to address the local disputes, weak state institutions and impunity that have helped sustain violence in eastern DRC. Without progress on those issues, a political agreement risks leaving the underlying causes of insecurity unresolved.
For residents, however, the immediate measure of progress is simpler: whether the fighting stops, essential services remain available and families can return home.
Chasumba said people were also waiting for those responsible for the destruction to address their losses.
“We are eager to see compensation for the damage caused by the war. Unfortunately, at this rate, we can see that we are in for a long-running saga, full of twists and turns,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Top IRGC commander in Iraq for talks amid Kataib Hezbollah tensions
noticias.resumen: Head of Iran's IRGC Quds Force to attend meetings over alleged oil smuggling linked to pro-Iranian armed groups.
noticias.texto:
Top IRGC commander in Iraq for talks amid Kataib Hezbollah tensions
Esmail Qaani, head of Iran’s IRGC Quds Force, has meetings over alleged oil smuggling linked to pro-Iranian armed groups.
The commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, has arrived in Iraq to push for a solution amid simmering tensions near the town of Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the pro-Iranian armed group Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi official has told Al Jazeera.
The Iraqi official explained that Qaani met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and held meetings with forces within the Coordination Framework—an umbrella for Shia Iraqi parties in the Iraqi parliament—in an effort to reach an agreement amid rising tensions over an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.
A leaked intelligence report last week had said two strategic oil pipelines running through the town of Jurf al-Nasr, located near Baghdad in the centre of the country, had effectively been tapped into.
Iraq recently launched a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.
While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, some analysts say they believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of pro-Iranian armed groups that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.
The Iraqi source told Al Jazeera that the judicial committee has not yet reached an agreement with the factions to enter the area.
At least three leaders of the Coordination Framework also expressed their rejection of any armed clash or entry of federal forces before reaching a political understanding with Kataib Hezbollah, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Iraq.
Iraq deploys army
On Monday, al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.
Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.
A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr.
A Kataib Hezbollah commander told AFP, “I can state decisively and with absolute certainty that the dream they dream of the Kataib withdrawing [from Jurf al-Nasr] will not come true, not even over our dead bodies.”
Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of armed groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.
The group has recently issued several statements criticising Iraq’s prime minister, accusing him of corruption and threatening his government.
It accused the government of “fabricating lies” about oil smuggling and of waging “the largest blackmail operation aimed at forcing” it to abandon its weapons.
Since coming into office, al-Zaidi has pledged to ensure that armed groups will hand over their weapons to the state.
