noticias.titulo: Venezuelan boxer Linares arrested in US and faces deportation, ICE confirms
noticias.resumen: The 41-year-old was detained on Sunday by US immigration authorities at El Paso International Airport in Texas.
noticias.texto:
Venezuelan boxer Linares arrested in US and faces deportation, ICE confirms
The 41-year-old was detained on Sunday by US immigration authorities at El Paso International Airport in Texas.
United States immigration authorities confirmed on Tuesday that former Venezuelan world boxing champion Jorge Linares remained in custody and was facing deportation proceedings after being detained on Sunday.
The 41-year-old was arrested by US Border Patrol agents and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials at El Paso International Airport, US media reported, citing an ICE spokesperson describing him as “a foreign national in the country without legal immigration status, arriving from Venezuela”.
“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” ICE said in a statement on Tuesday.
Three-time world champion Linares had announced his detention in a social media post on Sunday.
“ICE has detained me in El Paso, Texas. This is crazy,” Linares wrote on X. He has not posted anything since.
Al Jazeera was able to confirm through ICE’s online Detainee Locator System that Linares was being held at the El Paso Processing Centre.
Lawyers for the boxer said on Tuesday that Linares was “authorised” to be in the US.
“Mr Linares is authorised to be in the United States and he has cooperated fully with immigration authorities,” law firm Wilner & O’Reilly said.
“We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time.
“We are confident in Mr Linares’s position and ask his fans, the press and the public for patience in the meantime.”
The firm added that Linares and his family were deeply grateful for the outpouring of support from Venezuela and from fans around the world.
“Out of respect for his privacy and the legal process, we are unable to comment further on his case at this time,” the firm concluded.
World Boxing Association President Gilberto Mendoza also confirmed Linares’s detention and that immigration lawyers were handling his case.
“As WBA President, I will always support our champions, in and out of the ring. Stay strong, Jorge,” Mendoza wrote on X.
Widely regarded as one of the most skilful fighters of his generation, Linares won world titles in three weight divisions – featherweight, super featherweight and lightweight – during a 21-year career.
Nicknamed “The Golden Boy”, the Venezuelan won his first world title in 2007.
He would later hold the WBA super featherweight title from 2008 to 2009, and the WBA and WBC lightweight titles from 2014 to 2018.
He retired in 2023 following a defeat to Britain’s Jack Catterall in Liverpool, finishing his career with a record of 47 wins, 29 by knockout, and nine defeats.

noticias.titulo: ‘We want to go back’: Rohingya refugees pin hopes on ICJ genocide verdict
noticias.resumen: After almost a decade in exile, they're hoping the ICJ rules in their favour. But will that help them get back home?
noticias.texto:
‘We want to go back’: Rohingya refugees pin hopes on ICJ genocide verdict
After almost a decade in exile, they're hoping the ICJ rules in their favour. But will that help them get back home?
Cox’s Bazar/Dhaka, Bangladesh — When Dil Hossain and his wife, Alinnesa, fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State during the military crackdown on their Rohingya community in 2017, they carried their newborn daughter, Ishara, and ran for their lives.
Dil’s elderly parents could not escape and were killed as the family fled, along with several other relatives.
“We ran for our lives through mud, hills and water, with the baby tied to us,” Alinnesa recalls.
Nearly nine years later, Ishara is growing up in a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, far from the village where she was born. She has spent almost her entire life in exile. Her parents depend on humanitarian aid, which has declined sharply in recent years, and continue to wait for a chance to return home.
Now, the family is hoping the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya. On Thursday, the highest court of the United Nations is due to deliver its judgement in a landmark genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.
The Gambia filed the case on November 11, 2019, alleging that Myanmar had violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through acts committed against the Rohingya by its military and other security forces.
The allegations concern the so-called “clearance operations” that began in 2016 and escalated in August 2017, which The Gambia says involved genocidal acts intended to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part. The case asks the ICJ to determine Myanmar’s responsibility as a state under the convention.
“The court will find the truth. We suffered, so we know,” Dil said, expressing confidence that the judges would recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
More than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, most of them in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Many hope a ruling in their favour will bring recognition of their suffering and strengthen their claim to return home.
But even a landmark legal judgement in their favour may do little to change their lives immediately. Myanmar remains engulfed in civil war, with the same military that committed crimes against the Rohingya still in power, so the prospects for a safe return remain remote.
A life of ’24 hours of depression’ in exile
For many Rohingya refugees, nearly nine years in Bangladesh have brought a different kind of hardship: dependence on aid, uncertainty and a life far removed from the homes they left behind.
Nurul Amin, 25, who works with humanitarian groups in the camps, said the contrast between his former life in Myanmar and his present circumstances was stark.
“Back home, we had houses, big trees, gardens and farmland. We could grow our own food and did not have to depend on others. We were self-sufficient,” he said. “Here, we have to depend on others for almost everything. The difference is like that between heaven and earth.”
Years of displacement have also taken a toll on his mental wellbeing, he said. “It is 24 hours of depression. It feels as though we have lost our world, as though the world has abandoned us.”
Mohammad Rehan, now 18, was a child when the military crackdown began, but retains vivid memories that he says have left a lifelong mark.
“The most horrific thing I saw was houses being burned. It made me really afraid,” he said. “I was very young at the time, and those scenes left me traumatised.”
He hopes the court will recognise the Rohingya’s suffering and their right to equal treatment.
“If they find Myanmar guilty, I think it will help our community return and reclaim our rights,” he said.
What justice means for the Rohingya
The case brought by The Gambia accuses Myanmar of violating its obligations under the convention through the military’s treatment of the Rohingya, particularly during the 2017 crackdown.
For Rohingya leaders and activists, the ruling is more about whether the court recognises the crimes as genocide. They want their identity and rights restored, and those responsible held accountable.
Mohammad Zubair, chairman of the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights, said the community was confident the court would recognise what it had endured.
“They called us Bengali and committed genocide on us,” he said, referring to Myanmar’s refusal to even recognise the Rohingya as a community. “We witnessed the genocide with our own eyes. We suffered it. There has been enough evidence and testimony.”
Zubair said a favourable judgement could help pave the way for their return to Myanmar with dignity and rights. “The refugee life is worse than jail. There is no hope, and this is unbearable,” he said. “I have been a teacher for about two decades and was widely respected in Myanmar. Now I am living a refugee life. We want to go back.”
Nay San Lwin, a Rohingya activist and cofounder of the Free Rohingya Coalition, said meaningful justice would need more than just a court ruling.
“For us, meaningful justice is not simply a court verdict,” he said. “It means recognition of our identity, restoration of our rights, justice for every victim, and the opportunity to return to our homeland safely, rebuild our lives, and live in peace and dignity.”
That would require guarantees of citizenship, equal rights and recognition of the Rohingya as an ethnic community, he said. Refugees must also be able to return to their original villages and enjoy the same rights as other communities in Myanmar.
“If the court recognises that genocide took place against the Rohingya, the international community, including the United Nations, must ensure that the judgement is implemented without delay and that those responsible are held accountable,” Nay San Lwin said.
But even if the court does not find Myanmar responsible for genocide, he added, the struggle for justice would continue.
“Such a judgement would not erase our suffering or eliminate the need for accountability. Our commitment to justice does not depend on a single verdict,” Nay San Lwin said.
A landmark ruling, but what changes?
The judgement could have implications well beyond the Rohingya community.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for genocide. A ruling against Myanmar would therefore carry major implications for international law, said Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council.
It would also have consequences for Bangladesh, which has hosted the world’s largest Rohingya refugee population for years, he said. “If the court rules that the Rohingya were a victim of genocide, there will likely be ample pressure on Dhaka to provide more support and protections for Rohingya on their soil,” Kugelman said. “If the court doesn’t make this call, the pressure wouldn’t be as great.”
Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who has written extensively on the community, said a favourable judgement would formally recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya in 2017 within an international legal framework.
It would also give the community’s political demands a stronger legal basis, he said.
“The Rohingya crisis is often treated as a political bargaining issue. But once the court holds Myanmar accountable for genocide, those demands would have a stronger legal foundation,” he said. “There is a difference between making a political speech and having a legal judgement supporting your claims.”
The case could also reinforce the principle that countries not directly affected by atrocities can still bring a case under the Genocide Convention. The Gambia was not involved in the events in Myanmar, but brought the case before the court.
A ruling against Myanmar could therefore have implications for future cases involving alleged genocide elsewhere, Uddin said.
But he cautioned that the legal threshold for proving genocide is high. The court must establish that there was specific intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Myanmar has argued that its 2017 operations were counterinsurgency measures.
“I would not necessarily expect an entirely black-and-white judgement,” Uddin said. “The court may recognise some aspects of the case while subjecting others to legal scrutiny.”
A ruling that does not recognise the genocide allegation, he added, could strengthen what he calls the “politics of denial” and undermine confidence in international justice.
“I fear that genocide denial is now prevailing over the recognition of genocide around the world. This will give future atrocities a sense of impunity.”
Kugelman said a genocide finding could increase calls in the international community for further legal action against Myanmar’s military authorities. But he warned that the response from the country’s neighbours was likely to be more limited.
“As dramatic as a genocide verdict would be, Myanmar’s neighbours would likely continue to take a pragmatic position,” Kugelman said. “And of course this would redound to the regime’s benefit.”
The long road home
Even a favourable ICJ judgement would not guarantee the Rohingya a safe return to Myanmar.
The country’s civil war has transformed the balance of power in Rakhine State. The Arakan Army, a rebel group, has taken control of nearly all the state, including northern areas from which many Rohingya refugees fled.
Thomas Kean of the International Crisis Group said the group would be a necessary partner in any future repatriation discussions.
But relations between the Arakan Army and Rohingya communities have been badly damaged by the conflict, he said. In 2024, Rohingya armed groups fought alongside Myanmar’s military against the Arakan Army, while the military also conscripted Rohingya into militias. The Arakan Army has since been accused of abuses against Rohingya civilians, while Rohingya armed groups have carried out attacks in northern Rakhine.
“This violence has significantly undermined trust between the Rohingya, many of whom see the Arakan Army as equivalent [to], if not worse than, the Myanmar military, and the Arakan Army, which views the Rohingya as a potential security threat,” Kean said. “Lack of trust between the two sides is a major barrier to repatriation, and it could take years of patient work to improve the relationship.”
The ongoing fighting makes a return even more difficult, he said.
“The Arakan Army can hardly make guarantees around safety while a war is going on,” Kean said. “An end to the conflict in Rakhine would be the first step towards repatriation, but there would still be a long road ahead to making it happen.”
Kean also doubts how much additional leverage a genocide ruling would give the international community, when it comes to pressuring Myanmar’s military government.
Myanmar’s authorities have said they are willing to allow the Rohingya to return when security conditions permit. They have also indicated a willingness to grant citizenship, provided the refugees do not insist on being recognised as Rohingya.
He warned that a finding of genocide could instead make Myanmar’s military authorities more resistant to international pressure and lead to further restrictions on the work of the UN and other international organisations.
“I also fear that a genocide finding against Myanmar would only make Naypyidaw more recalcitrant,” he said, referring to Myanmar’s administrative capital. “I think there’s also a risk of a broader backlash within Myanmar, or among Myanmar people, many of whom likely still see the Rohingya as illegal immigrants.”
That concern also finds an echo among Rohingya refugees. Rohingya youth Nurul Amin said a favourable judgement should not be seen as a victory for the community alone.
“There are many other ethnic communities in Myanmar that are also under attack. We want them to live in peace, with democracy restored, and to coexist,” he said. “We want justice and our rights back. But we also want all the ethnic communities in Myanmar to be able to live peacefully, without fear of the military.”
Nasir Uddin said the judgement could provide legal recognition and generate international pressure on Myanmar. But it could not itself bring the refugees home.
“We should not assume that a favourable ICJ judgement means the Rohingya will return home the next day,” he said. “These things take time. Nothing will change overnight.”
Kean said Bangladesh would also need to engage with the different actors in Myanmar’s conflict rather than rely on one side alone. Dhaka should establish a channel for sustained dialogue with the Arakan Army, particularly on repatriation, border security, trade and humanitarian assistance, he said.
For Dil and Alinnesa, however, the question is more immediate. Will their daughter ever have the chance to grow up in the country where she was born, with the rights and security her parents lost?
“We have lost our lives, our properties and our people,” Alinnesa said. “The refugee life we are living here has no future for us and our kids. We want to return to our homes and live our lives in peace.”

noticias.titulo: Epstein’s death more likely homicide than suicide, forensic expert says
noticias.resumen: An analysis of autopsy records and photos suggests the US sex offender was murdered in 2019, an expert says.
noticias.texto:
Epstein’s death more likely homicide than suicide, forensic expert says
An analysis of autopsy records and photos suggests the US sex offender was murdered in 2019, an expert says.
Forensic experts claim Epstein was strangled to death
A forensic expert has analysed autopsy records and photos that he believes suggest US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was murdered rather than died by suicide.
Following a years-long investigation, Michael Freeman, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine, told the CBS News broadcaster that he had concluded that Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind, while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges in 2019.
“The injuries that were documented by the medical examiner were not consistent with the suicidal hanging,” Freeman said on Monday.
“If you put it all together, it is most consistent with a homicidal strangulation from behind using a narrow knotted fabric ligature,” he added.
Epstein was found hanging in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York on August 10, 2019. An autopsy concluded that he had taken his own life.
His death has long been the subject of conspiracy theories, with some claiming he was killed over fears he would provide damning evidence linking prominent public figures to cases of sexual abuse, rape and paedophilia.
Security cameras outside Epstein’s cell were not working on the day of his death. A 2023 Department of Justice report concluded that the facility had longstanding problems with its cameras.
Epstein’s brother, Mark, has called for a new investigation following Freeman’s comments. Freeman argued on Monday that the evidence suggests Epstein was strangled with a ligature, which was then used to suspend his body from a bunk bed.
The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner said it “stands by its determination”.

noticias.titulo: China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
noticias.resumen: The president says Beijing seeks to provide a 'stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises'.
noticias.texto:
China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
The president says Beijing seeks to provide a ‘stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises’.
China’s President Xi Jinping has urged support for “free and open trade”, pitching Beijing as a stable partner – as opposed to President Donald Trump-led Washington – and pledging to stand up to trade protectionism.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen, southern China, Xi took aim at rising “unilateralism and protectionism”.
His remarks appeared to be a veiled criticism of Trump’s America First policies, under which the United States has imposed tariffs on both allies and economic rivals.
Xi is due to meet Trump, who is travelling from the Philippines for the APEC leaders’ summit later on Wednesday. Xi and Trump are then due to hold an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Xi told business executives that the Asia Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
Trump’s America First approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone.
Washington also limits Chinese access to leading-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help power artificial intelligence (AI).
“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” Xi said.
He added that China sought to “provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises” and would continue to expand access in its manufacturing and services sectors.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access, and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told the Associated Press news agency that Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia, or the US directly.
Xi’s message is “likely to resonate with many Global South countries, and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington”, Chen added.

noticias.titulo: Photos: India defeat Pakistan to win SAFF Championship in Bangladesh
noticias.resumen: Thousands of Bangladeshi fans turned up to watch India complete a three-peat of SAFF titles in Dhaka.
noticias.texto:
In Pictures
Photos: India defeat Pakistan to win SAFF Championship in Bangladesh
Thousands of Bangladeshi fans turned up to watch India complete a three-peat of SAFF titles with a last-gasp win over Pakistan in Dhaka.
On an evening of thrilling action, on-field drama and passionate support in the stands, India defeated Pakistan 2-1 to win the South Asian Football Federation (SAFF) Championship in Bangladesh.
While Bangladesh fans were left heartbroken with the home team’s semifinal loss, they turned up in the thousands to watch the archrivals compete in a closely fought final at the National Stadium in Dhaka on Tuesday.
A large majority of fans chanted their support for Pakistan, saying it was their second favourite team after Bangladesh. Others backed India after Pakistan’s ouster of the home team.
A Palestine flag was also spotted in the stands.
Bangladeshi fan Anwar Hossain came to the stadium with a Palestinian flag draped over his shoulders. While he rooted for Pakistan in the final, he told Al Jazeera he was supporting Palestine because he was “against hegemony”.
“India is a hegemonic country that wants to dominate its neighbouring countries. To stand against occupation and to support independence, I’m supporting Pakistan tonight.”
More than 10,000 fans watched the match at the National Stadium in Dhaka, but several complained that local organisers did not advertise or promote the tournament well.
Once the match kicked off, Pakistan took the lead just before the end of the first half with a goal from Alamgir Ghazi to spark celebrations on the pitch and in the crowd.
Not long after play resumed, Pakistani defender Junaid Shah received a straight red card for a high, studs-up tackle. Down to 10 men, Pakistan could not maintain their lead, and India’s Suhail Bhat soon found an equaliser.
The match seemed to be headed for extra time before Sandip Mandi headed in a winner for India in the 90th minute.
India won the trophy for the third consecutive time, and the 10th overall, to retain the title of South Asia’s best men’s football team.

noticias.titulo: Russia, China should ‘lead’ push to multipolar world, Xi tells APEC summit
noticias.resumen: Putin says Western powers are 'former hegemons', with Europe in the midst of a 'humiliating decline'.
noticias.texto:
Russia, China should ‘lead’ push to multipolar world, Xi tells APEC summit
Putin says Western powers are ‘former hegemons’, with Europe in the midst of a ‘humiliating decline’.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has said that Beijing and Moscow should “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Xi and Putin held bilateral discussions on Wednesday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Following Xi, Putin took to the stage, telling the summit that Western powers were “former hegemons”, adding that Europe was in the midst of a “humiliating decline”.
“Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having lost much of their intimidating power,” Putin said.
“While sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth – let alone crushing the economies of competitors.”
Russia’s economy has been heavily sanctioned by the US and Europe because of its war against Ukraine, which began in February 2022 when Moscow invaded its neighbour.
Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Shenzhen, said that both Xi and Putin called for a “more fair and multipolar world order and that the two leaders also said they would maintain close ties amid what they both described as global uncertainty”.
She added that Xi and Putin “have a close personal relationship, and they have met more than 40 times over the years, and these two countries are also strategically aligned”, with China remaining Russia’s biggest trading partner, and Russia providing Beijing with much-needed energy resources.
“Putin clearly took a swing at European countries, in particular, that have put sanctions on Russia,” Yu added.
But in Shenzhen, “Putin is having a bit of a moment in the sun” at the APEC summit, where he is being treated as a guest of honour.
Differing expectations
Robert Kelly, a professor of political science at Pusan National University in South Korea’s Busan, said that all three leaders are “coming in with fairly different expectations and desires of what they want”.
“That’s going to make it quite difficult for them to actually find an agreement,” he said. “Nuclear weapons is an area where the three leaders could really make some great progress,” he argued, adding that the current “tripolar world of nuclear powers is different than the Cold War”.
“It would be great if the three of them could actually bring [the arms race] under control,” Kelly told Al Jazeera.
“But all the different parties are in different places – for the Russians, their weapons are very important to bolster their perception as a great power, despite their problems in Ukraine,” he noted.
“The Chinese have engaged in a major buildup, and it doesn’t look like they want arms control, nuclear weapons at least in their 10 years; and the United States has been sort of very standoffish about any kind of deal,” Kelly said.
“There’s a very strong public goods argument for a positive outcome, for an arms control agreement, but it just won’t happen,” he added.
APEC was established in 1989 and has 21 members, accounting for more than 50 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and representing about 2.7 billion people.
The organisation aims to support economic growth and prosperity in the Asia Pacific region.
Leaders are expected to discuss a range of important issues at this year’s summit, including artificial intelligence (AI) and trade – two areas in which the US and China play dominant roles.
A key issue for APEC members and the wider world is the trade truce between Washington and Beijing, and whether it will be extended beyond January.

noticias.titulo: Hungry, unpaid and afraid: Africa’s journalists pushed to the brink
noticias.resumen: The exploitation of journalists is undermining independent reporting and the public’s right to know.
noticias.texto:
Hungry, unpaid and afraid: Africa’s journalists pushed to the brink
The exploitation of journalists is undermining independent reporting and the public’s right to know.
How can a hungry journalist be expected to deliver the facts the public needs? Across Africa, journalists are struggling to survive, working for months without pay and reporting without contracts or protection. This is not just a workplace crisis. It is an attack on the very conditions that make independent journalism possible.
Yet journalists are expected to expose corruption, scrutinise power and verify claims while wondering how they will pay for food, rent or transport to their next assignment. For many, journalism has become a struggle for survival. The consequences are visible in every delayed salary, every unpaid assignment and every story abandoned because the reporter cannot afford to pursue it.
With UNESCO’s support, the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) and its affiliated unions and associations across Africa’s five regions carried out the first journalist-led, continent-wide survey of journalists’ working conditions, labour rights, safety and media freedom. It drew responses from 1,586 journalists in 45 African countries. Among those surveyed, 61 percent said their income from journalism did not meet their basic living needs, 58 percent reported delayed salaries and 62 percent had no written contracts.
Behind these numbers are journalists expected to perform an essential public service without the means to make a decent living. In Central Africa, 55 percent of respondents reported salary arrears lasting three to eight months within a single year.
The deprivation extends beyond pay. Many respondents also reported having no health insurance or paid leave. Freelancers and contributors are among the most exposed. Many lack contracts, predictable incomes and social protections yet are expected to produce regular work and take risks similar to those faced by newsroom staff.
This widespread precarity is corroding the quality of journalism. Investigations require time, travel, secure communications, access to documents and careful verification. Poverty and unpaid work deprive reporters of these basic tools. A newsroom under financial strain has less capacity to check claims, protect sources and follow a story beyond the first official statement. Stories are dropped. Errors are harder to catch. The public is left with a thinner, weaker account of events.
The consequences for information integrity are grave. The FAJ report describes journalists relying on side businesses, borrowed money and allowances from outside sources, including political “per diems”. This does not mean that journalists in precarious work are dishonest. It means poverty wages and financial exposure can create openings for outside interests to influence what gets covered and how. These conditions can allow “brown envelope” practices to flourish. When a journalist’s ability to survive depends on money from a person or institution with a stake in a story, independent reporting is placed under pressure.
The survey shows that these abysmal conditions are already shaping coverage. Eighty-four percent of respondents said they practised self-censorship frequently or occasionally. Sixty-nine percent said threats had led them to avoid certain stories. When a journalist fears losing an already inadequate income, censorship does not need to arrive as a formal ban. It can be the decision not to investigate because the personal cost feels too high.
The danger is physical as well as economic. Sixty-five percent of journalists who took part in the survey had experienced work-related threats or intimidation in the previous three years. More than half rarely or never felt safe reporting, and 78 percent said they had no workplace access to legal support. Journalists are sent to report on dangerous events and uncover uncomfortable truths that powerful interests would rather keep hidden, then are left to face the perilous consequences alone.
Online attacks deepen the crisis. Journalists reported online harassment, digital surveillance and hacking attempts, often without access to digital safety training. Female journalists face additional risks, including sexual harassment, online gender-based violence, unequal pay and exclusion from leadership. When women are driven out of public debate by threats, journalism loses their reporting and the public loses the perspectives they bring. The strain is also evident in journalists’ wellbeing: 44 percent reported frequent burnout, and 47 percent had considered leaving journalism.
The survey’s regional findings highlight delayed or inadequate pay in West, Central and Southern Africa and political intimidation, arrests and legal harassment in East and North Africa. There is no single African newsroom experience: In some places poverty is the most immediate threat; in others, repression and physical danger dominate. Often journalists face both.
Country examples also show that democratic credentials alone do not guarantee decent conditions. The report describes Ghana as having relatively strong democratic credentials yet cites research from 2023 finding that many media workers there earned as little as G500 cedis ($38.80) to 1,000 cedis ($77.61) a month. Freelancers often relied on transport reimbursements, commissions or sponsored content to survive. Elections and democratic institutions matter, but without labour rights, fair pay and protection from pressure, journalists can remain economically vulnerable even in a more open political environment.
There are, however, practical examples of progress. In Mauritania, a government decision in 2025 regularised 1,860 media workers at public media institutions after a sustained campaign by the Association of Mauritanian Journalists with the backing of FAJ and the International Federation of Journalists. These journalists gained permanent contracts, equal pay and benefits, medical coverage, paid leave and retirement benefits after more than 30 years of campaigning for professional and social recognition. In Morocco, a collective agreement signed in February 2023 and negotiated by the National Syndicate of Moroccan Journalists secured a net monthly salary increase of 2,000 dirhams ($201) for eligible journalists with more than four years of experience. These changes show how government action and collective bargaining can put real protections into journalists’ working lives.
Namibia offers another important lesson. Journalists in the survey still described long hours, unpaid overtime and stagnant salaries. But formal registration of the Namibia Media Professionals Union gave media workers a recognised way to organise and bargain collectively. This month, the union secured a substantially improved settlement for workers facing retrenchment at The Namibian newspaper. This does not resolve the wider crisis, but it shows how collective representation can defend workers’ rights in practice.
In Somalia, long one of Africa’s most dangerous countries for journalists, the National Union of Somali Journalists led the development of a national action plan on journalists’ safety adopted in September 2022 after consultations involving journalists, the government and international partners. It sets out a Somali-led framework to strengthen journalists’ safety, media freedom, access to information and protection for female journalists. Its adoption was an important step towards safer working conditions for journalists.
Across the continent, the African Union and its organs have also taken steps to address journalists’ safety and media freedom. Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU commissioner for political affairs, peace and security, has been a vocal advocate for media freedom and journalists’ safety and a leading voice in affirming that professional media are indispensable to democracy and good governance. Over the past three years, the AU Peace and Security Council has increasingly addressed Africa’s media environment. In October, it called for greater protection of journalists, action against impunity and stronger safeguards for access to information.
These examples show what governments, media organisations and multilateral institutions must do. Enforce labour protections. Pay wages on time. Provide written contracts, social protection and legal support. Protect the right to organise and bargain collectively. Treat freelance journalists as workers with enforceable labour rights. Investigate attacks and stop using laws to intimidate reporters. Democratic safeguards and labour protections must advance together. Neither can substitute for the other.
When journalists are forced to choose between pursuing the truth and securing their own survival, the public pays the price: Investigations go unfinished, abuses escape scrutiny and vital facts remain hidden. Fair pay, secure employment and safety are essential to media freedom and the public’s right to know.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Africa’s economic future cannot depend on Washington
noticias.resumen: Trump's move to exclude South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA shows why Africa must accelerate its own economic integration.
noticias.texto:
Africa’s economic future cannot depend on Washington
Trump’s move to exclude South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA shows why Africa must accelerate its own economic integration.
On September 2 , United States President Donald Trump signed legislation extending the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) through the end of 2028, following overwhelming support in Congress. Yet just two months later, on November 2 , his administration announced plans to terminate the eligibility of South Africa and Rwanda for the programme from January 1, 2027.
The decision lays bare the fundamental weakness of AGOA: African economies depend on trade privileges that Washington can withdraw whenever its political priorities change.
AGOA is a US trade law that currently covers 33 eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It was enacted on May 18, 2000, to allow these countries to export thousands of products to the US market duty-free, and was promoted as a strategic mechanism to foster economic growth, expand trade between the US and the continent and encourage economic and political reforms.
AGOA initially delivered promising results. It is estimated to have supported more than 300,000 direct jobs across Africa and 1.3 million indirect jobs. According to a 2024 US Trade Representative report, two-way goods trade between the US and sub-Saharan Africa reached $47.5bn in 2023, including $9.7bn in imports under AGOA and the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP), of which $5.5bn consisted of non-oil products such as apparel and agricultural goods.
However, recent figures point to growing challenges, with some even suggesting a decline. A Congressional Research Service report shows that US imports receiving AGOA duty-free treatment dropped sharply from $7.9bn in 2024 to $5bn in 2025. Another analysis by the German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) noted that the share of US imports from sub-Saharan Africa benefiting from AGOA and GSP preferences plummeted from more than 80 percent in 2008 to roughly 24.7 percent in 2021 amid eligibility uncertainty and short renewal windows.
Only a few eligible sub-Saharan African countries capture most of the programme’s benefits. South Africa is its largest beneficiary, with exports to the US worth billions of dollars annually, while most other eligible countries struggle to make full use of its preferences.
Furthermore, because the US administers the programme’s preferences unilaterally, rather than through a bilateral treaty, Washington can exclude or reinstate any eligible country based on its own assessments and criteria, including market reforms, human rights and labour standards.
Since the programme’s inception, some countries suspended from AGOA have criticised the impact of their removal. Ethiopia’s suspension in 2022, for instance, led to the loss of thousands of garment sector jobs.
In practice, Washington’s geopolitical interests often carry more weight in eligibility decisions than AGOA’s stated criteria.
The Trump administration’s decision to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s AGOA eligibility is a clear case in point. Both countries have pursued policies that conflict with Washington’s interests and that the administration regards as a threat. South Africa has strengthened its economic and political ties with US rivals such as China and Russia, while facing accusations from Washington of obstructing American trade and investment, alongside Trump’s allegations of a “white genocide”.
Rwanda’s alleged support for the M23 rebel group in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has also brought it into conflict with US interests in the region’s critical minerals.
Sharp declines in AGOA import values, unstable US trade policies, and short-term extensions leave African exporters highly vulnerable. Losing AGOA access triggers immediate customs setbacks, including tariff increases of 15 to 20 percent on some products. Ultimately, these unpredictable extensions prevent AGOA from building a self-sustaining African industrial base, making accelerated implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) an urgent priority for the continent.
Africa’s economic vision cannot remain hostage to changing administrations’ policies or unilateral decisions made abroad, as the continent needs to build strategic resilience and economic independence. The AfCFTA is a historic trade agreement signed under the auspices of the African Union (AU) on March 21, 2018, in Kigali, Rwanda, which officially entered into force on May 30, 2019, with trading beginning on January 1, 2021.
The agreement aims to bring African Union member states into a unified market of over 1.3 billion people, with a combined gross domestic product (GDP) exceeding $3.4 trillion.
Relying on a vast regional market would mitigate the impact of external shocks, such as the revocation of preferential trade agreements like AGOA or the sudden imposition of steep tariffs. Given that trade between African nations currently accounts for only about 15–18 percent of the continent’s total trade, the AfCFTA aims to progressively eliminate tariffs on 90 percent of tariff lines, thereby stimulating internal commerce and providing a buffer against declines in Western markets caused by tariff fluctuations.
AGOA and many other external agreements have largely kept Africa in the role of a raw material supplier. In contrast, the AfCFTA encourages the development of regional value chains, where one African nation might produce raw materials, another processes them into finished goods, and the final product is sold to consumers within the continent, with fewer tariff barriers.
AfCFTA has made notable progress in developing the instruments needed for continental trade. The number of countries participating in trade initiatives under the agreement has grown to include South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Tunisia, making use of its preferential tariff arrangements.
The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), launched on January 13, 2022, enables banks and financial institutions to conduct cross-border transactions in African currencies, reducing reliance on foreign currencies such as the US dollar.
The African Union also adopted protocols on competition policy in February 2023 and digital trade in February 2024, aimed at promoting fair competition and facilitating e-commerce. In August 2026, the AfCFTA Secretariat signed an agreement to modernise and digitise customs systems. The AfCFTA Adjustment Fund has also been activated, with an estimated financing requirement of $8bn–$10bn, to support developing countries and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as they adapt to the requirements of the single market.
For AfCFTA to serve its purpose and reduce dependence on volatile global trade agreements that prioritise Western interests over those of Africa, the continent still needs to accelerate economic integration by removing tariff and non-tariff barriers and harmonising trade and regulatory policies to facilitate the smooth movement of goods and services.
To improve local markets, African countries must undertake the costly and risky investments involved in building cross-border infrastructure to reduce the cost of moving goods and services between African countries. Digital energy grids will be essential to this infrastructure, alongside roads and railways.
Africa must shift from simply exporting raw materials to building strong regional value chains focused on local manufacturing and innovation. Meeting the needs of the continent’s vast market would strengthen its economic self-sufficiency and reduce its vulnerability to external political decisions and the expiration of unilateral trade agreements.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemen
noticias.resumen: The Houthis’ expanding war economy fuels military recruitment while poverty deepens and public services deteriorate.
noticias.texto:
How the Houthis fund war effort and tighten grip on Yemen
The Houthis’ expanding war economy fuels military recruitment while poverty deepens and public services deteriorate.
Sanaa, Yemen – Mohammed, 19, joined the fighting on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in March this year, battling alongside Houthi forces. The fighting has been relentless over the past few months, as the Houthis advance. The Houthis have faced pro-government forces, as well as Saudi-led coalition air strikes.
They have also faced international sanctions and attempts by Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government to restrict their access to funds.
And yet, speaking during a recent visit to Sanaa, Mohammed said the Houthis were able to continue getting supplies to their fighters.
“It is not always war and death on the battlefield. We have a good time. We eat the best food. We can chew khat. If injured or sick, we will be taken care of. Our commander on the ground makes sure we have the supplies we need,” Mohammed told Al Jazeera.
Throughout a decade of war, Yemen’s Houthi group has developed a range of funding streams, which have enabled it to finance its military operations and tighten its grip on areas under its control.
The Mokha Center for Strategic Studies said in a July report this year that the Houthi financial system generates direct and indirect financial resources and costs worth approximately $2.5bn annually.
That includes around $800m from taxes and customs, $600m from additional fees and levies, $300m from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort, and about $100m linked to mobilisation events, according to the report.
A May research paper from the same institution estimated that nearly 60 percent of collected revenues in Houthi-controlled areas are directed to the security and military sectors.
Diverse funding techniques
As the Houthis’ war grinds on against Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi-led coalition forces, Houthi authorities have employed more fund-generating techniques. Ali Naji, a Sanaa resident, often receives messages on his mobile phone, urging him to contribute to the missile and drone air forces.
“I do not contribute, but thousands of people do, even with 100 Yemeni riyals [$0.19 at the exchange rate set by Houthi authorities in Sanaa]. When these small contributions add up, they make millions, and this funds the war efforts,” Naji, a father of three, told Al Jazeera.
Another method is distributing envelopes to solicit contributions. Last week, Naji was watching the funeral procession of more than 40 civilians who were killed in Sanaa in what the Houthis said were Saudi air strikes.
A Houthi member approached him and handed him an envelope, requesting that he give a voluntary contribution to the war effort. “I did not feel comfortable refusing or returning it empty. I put 1,000 Yemeni riyals (around $1.90) inside the envelope and gave it back.”
When mass rallies are held, a large sheet of cloth is spread on the ground, and people can contribute what they can. “Some give cash. Some donate weapons such as rifles and pistols, or jambiyas [traditional daggers]. From one rally, millions of Yemeni riyals can be raised,” said Naji.
In addition, imported oil has been a major source of revenue for the Yemeni group. In January, the US Department of the Treasury said the Iranian government sold and provided a free monthly shipment of oil to the Houthis using Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates.
With the shipments of Iranian oil, the Houthis continued to acquire a significant amount of revenue through illicit oil sales, generating over $2bn annually, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Financing recruitment
Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Houthis have established a self-reinforcing system in which “economic control finances coercion, and coercion enables further economic control”.
Their income sources include taxes, customs duties, zakat religious levies, and additional levies, and fuel and telecommunications, said Al-Jeddawy.
“Their control over import permits, fees, and access to foreign currency also gives them considerable leverage over traders and businesses. These resources sustain the security apparatus and patronage networks through which the movement enforces compliance and consolidates its authority,” he added.
Al-Jeddawy noted that the Houthi financial system supports recruitment amid shrinking employment opportunities and unpaid public-sector salaries.
“Joining Houthi forces has become one of the few sources of income available to some young men. Recruitment is accompanied by ideological indoctrination, extending the movement’s influence from military camps into families and local communities. Economic deprivation therefore does more than facilitate mobilisation: it helps the group militarise everyday life and reinforce their authority at the social level.”
A 2024 United Nations panel of experts estimated that Houthi fighters numbered around 350,000, bolstered by the recruitment of fighters sometimes aged under 18.
These resources fund more than recruitment and mobilisation. “The group has expanded its security apparatus, developed increasingly sophisticated weapons, and invested in fortifications, trenches, tunnels, underground facilities, and weapons workshops. This level of continuous militarisation requires considerable and sustained expenditure,” said Al-Jeddawy.
The cost to civilians
Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, said Houthi-run civilian institutions are starved of funds, salaries are not paid regularly, and basic services, such as health and education, continue to deteriorate.
“About one million Yemeni public employees have not received their salaries regularly since 2016. Meanwhile, the group has developed its arsenal and funded its war efforts. When war is a priority, the living conditions of the population become miserable,” Saleh told Al Jazeera.
Roughly 80 percent of the population in Yemen lives below the poverty line, and nearly 22.3 million people depend on some form of humanitarian assistance, according to United Nations reports.
For Mohammed, the Houthi soldier, funding military operations is “a duty” and “a long-term investment”.
“Liberating the country and expelling foreign forces is not free,” said Mohammed. “So, funding fighters and military operations should be every patriot’s priority.”

noticias.titulo: What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season
noticias.resumen: India and Pakistan had 42 of the world’s 50 most polluted cities in 2025. Millions now face another toxic winter.
noticias.texto:
What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season
India and Pakistan had 42 of the world’s 50 most polluted cities in 2025. Millions now face another toxic winter.
As winter approaches in the Northern Hemisphere, so does smog season, and few places are hit harder than South Asia.
Cities across the region, from New Delhi to Dhaka, are blanketed in a thick grey haze, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeding 350 in several parts of India’s capital last week, a level classed as “hazardous”, according to the air quality monitoring platform IQAir.
In winter, a layer of warmer air can trap cooler air near the ground. Combined with low wind speeds, this stops pollution from vehicles, industry and crop burning from dispersing.
Al Jazeera visualises which cities have the worst air quality, how it is measured, how smog affects your health and what you can do to protect yourself.
What causes smog?
Smog mostly comes from burning fossil fuels, particularly coal, along with exhaust from vehicles and factories, and smoke from forest and crop fires.
Summer smog and winter smog form differently. In summer, sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and other pollutants to form ground-level ozone. In winter, a layer of warm air can sit on top of cooler air near the ground, trapping pollution and stopping it from dispersing.
In South Asia, winter smog is made worse by geography. The Indo-Gangetic Plain, which stretches across parts of Pakistan, northern India, Nepal and Bangladesh, is one of the world’s most polluted regions. Hemmed in by the Himalayas to the north, the plain has weak winds and a shallow layer of air in winter, so pollution has nowhere to go.
How is air quality measured?
The air we breathe is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, but it also contains small amounts of other gases and tiny particles, some of which are harmful.
Monitoring stations track six main pollutants, including ozone, nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter (PM), tiny particles suspended in the air.
The most harmful is PM2.5, particles 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter, about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They can travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.
These readings are combined into an Air Quality Index (AQI). The US AQI runs from 0 to 500 and is split into six colour-coded categories:
- Green (0-50), good: little or no risk.
- Yellow (51-100), moderate: acceptable for most people.
- Orange (101-150), unhealthy for sensitive groups: children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions.
- Red (151-200), unhealthy: the general public may be affected.
- Purple (201-300), very unhealthy: health risks for everyone.
- Maroon (301+), hazardous: emergency conditions.
Which cities have the most polluted air?
All 50 of the world’s most polluted cities in 2025 were in Asia, according to IQAir, with 42 of them in India and Pakistan.
Loni, on the outskirts of Delhi in Uttar Pradesh state, topped the list with average PM2.5 levels of 112.5 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic metre), more than 22 times the WHO’s recommended limit, followed by Hotan in China and Byrnihat and New Delhi in India.
Vehicles account for 23 percent of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 percent, according to India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The four Chinese cities on the list are in Xinjiang, where desert dust is a major source.
How does pollution affect your health?
Air pollution, both outdoors and inside homes, is linked to about seven million premature deaths worldwide each year, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Pollutants mainly enter the body through the lungs, where they can cause inflammation, damage cells and weaken the immune system. PM2.5 can also pass into the bloodstream, reaching organs including the heart and brain.
Air pollution is most strongly linked to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer and pneumonia. It can also worsen asthma and reduce lung function, while smoke from cooking with fossil fuels indoors is linked to cataracts.
Long-term exposure has also been linked to dementia and a higher risk of diabetes.
Children, older people, pregnant women and those with heart or lung conditions are most at risk. Exposure during pregnancy has been linked to premature birth and low birth weight.
What can you do to protect yourself?
You can’t control the air outside, but these simple steps can reduce how much pollution you breathe in:
- Wear a mask: Use a well-fitting N95 or similar mask outdoors, as cloth masks offer little protection against fine particles.
- Keep indoor air clean: Close windows on high-pollution days and use an air purifier with a HEPA filter.
- Limit outdoor activity: Avoid strenuous exercise outside on high-pollution days.
- Check air quality: Check the Air Quality Index (AQI) in a weather app before going out.
- Protect those most at risk: Take extra care with children, older people and those with asthma.
How governments are tackling pollution
Governments are trying a range of measures to cut air pollution, particularly in large cities.
Car-free days close city centres to vehicles or limit driving by number plate. Paris held its first car-free day in September 2015, covering about a third of the city. Nitrogen dioxide levels fell by up to 40 percent in some areas, according to monitoring agency Airparif. From 2016, the city also began closing the Avenue de Champs-Elysees to traffic on the first Sunday of each month.
Low-emission zones charge the most polluting vehicles. Within three months of London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) launching in 2019, nitrogen dioxide concentrations at roadside monitoring sites in central London fell by 19.6 percent, according to a University of Birmingham study.
Some cities have targeted household fuel burning. Krakow, Poland, replaced more than 25,000 coal and wood-burning heating devices before banning solid fuels for home heating in September 2019. Average annual PM2.5 levels in the city fell by 40 percent between 2010 and 2021, according to a 2025 study.

noticias.titulo: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
noticias.resumen: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
