Hostility towards the media has been a hallmark of both of Trump’s terms in office. He has tried to ban outlets that broadcast critical coverage from the White House and accused a large number of journalists of reporting fake news.

noticias.titulo: Hacked fridges show the cost of 'vintage' infrastructure, and AI makes it worse, says Cisco executive
noticias.resumen: The real cyber threat is ageing infrastructure as well as AI, a Cisco executive tells Euronews Next.
noticias.texto:
The real cyber threat is ageing infrastructure as well as AI, a Cisco executive tells Euronews Next.
This year proved that no device is too ordinary to be a target. Even smart fridges have been easily hacked, with devastating consequences.
Dozens of European supermarkets saw fridge and freezer temperatures turned up in early November, following a cyber attack in France in October.
It shows a start cybersecurity reality: the biggest threats are not new hacking techniques but an old infrastructure problem combined with the speed at which artificial intelligence can uncover weaknesses across connected devices.
"These are not new or novel hacks… These are exploiting things that have a bit of underlying vulnerability," said Anthony Grieco, chief security and trust officer at global technology company Cisco.
“And it is that ability to discover it... The fridges are an interesting example because it just shows you the breadth and scale that you have to think about and operate in," he told Euronews Next.
Smart fridges are just one small example of other connected devices that are at risk. Grieco warned that a far more dangerous version of the same problem is unfolding inside critical infrastructure, with hospital medical devices and factory assembly lines, water utilities and digital networks also at risk.
Many of these essential systems run on ageing "end-of-life" hardware and software that manufacturers no longer support with security updates.
"If you're driving around in a 30-year-old vehicle, you probably can't go and buy the brake pads for that vehicle from the original manufacturer anymore," Grieco said.
"There are many critical infrastructure systems that just keep working, but are end of life and end of support. And the risk equation on that has changed dramatically in the last six months… We have too many critical infrastructure systems that are running that you would call vintage," he added.
To minimise those risks, he urges companies to focus on enforcing stronger credentials and passwords, and to retire the "vintage tech" that can no longer receive updates, segmenting environments, and patching faster.
AI fighting AI
But cybersecurity is being threatened by artificial intelligence as the technology uncovers long-hidden software flaws at machine speed, automates attacks, and becomes more human, leading people to give away sensitive information.
"When we look at what adversaries are doing, they're starting to use AI tools and agents to compromise systems and compromise the IT systems that are out there," Grieco said.
This shows them being able to "do things at a pace and speed that would have taken humans a lot longer to do in the past," he added.
But he said AI is also helping cybersecurity defenders in that you can flip the script so the technology is used to counter threats.
"We’re using AI to defend at a pace and scale that we haven’t been able to before," he said.
Cisco is working alongside partners, using frontier models from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, to find and patch flaws before criminals can exploit them.
Earlier this year, Cisco said that its teams used AI tools to scan 1.8 billion lines of source code in just eight weeks, a massive milestone that would have otherwise taken human engineers roughly eight years.
AI is also eliminating the "noise" of false alarms that has long plagued security teams, pinpointing genuine threats with near 100% efficacy so engineers can immediately fix real risks, he said.
"There are real things that can be done today," Grieco said, adding that no matter how clever AI gets, suspicious network activity can still be seen and stopped.
"Ultimately, the bits on the wire don't lie," he said.

noticias.titulo: ECB draws parallels between AI boom and dotcom bubble as tech giants pile on debt
noticias.resumen: The European Central Bank drew parallels between the AI boom and the dotcom bubble in its Financial Stability Review on Wednesday, warning that a wave of large IPOs could signal late-cycle exuberance as tech giants pile on debt, leaving markets exposed to an abrupt sell-off.
noticias.texto:
The European Central Bank drew parallels between the AI boom and the dotcom bubble in its Financial Stability Review on Wednesday, warning that a wave of large IPOs could signal late-cycle exuberance as tech giants pile on debt, leaving markets exposed to an abrupt sell-off.
The European Central Bank compared the AI boom with the dotcom bubble in its biannual Financial Stability Review on Wednesday, warning that a surge in stock market listings may point to late-cycle exuberance while tech giants borrow heavily, leaving markets vulnerable to a sudden sell-off.
Risks to the eurozone's financial stability "remain elevated, given persistent geoeconomic uncertainty and growing exposure to AI," said ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić, who had sounded a similar warning on Monday.
The report comes a day after the European Commission said the EU economy had weathered the Iran war's energy shock better than expected. The ECB agrees, but warns that the AI optimism helping the economy has itself become a risk.
Echoes of the dotcom era
Share prices rest on "extraordinarily strong earnings expectations" for AI firms that may prove hard to meet, the report said, warning that cheaper AI models could undercut today's market leaders.
With AI spending now outstripping the cash their businesses generate, US tech giants are borrowing at a record pace, increasingly in euros, leaving European investors more exposed.
The ECB estimates that big tech firms had more than $4 trillion (€3.63tn) in off-balance-sheet commitments by the end of the second quarter of 2026, debt-like obligations that are not recorded as liabilities, while chipmakers often finance the customers buying their chips.
The central bank stopped short of calling the AI boom a bubble, but said such a rapid shift to debt invites comparisons with both the dotcom and subprime mortgage bubbles of the early 2000s.
Meanwhile, the amount raised by US IPOs is on track to beat their dotcom-era high relative to the size of the economy, and similar booms have tended to come near market peaks, the ECB said.
ECB staff estimate they will raise around $212 billion (€192bn) this year, up from about $44bn (€40bn) in 2025, according to the report.
SpaceX's record IPO in June led the way. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, is expected to set its IPO price on Wednesday and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.
Big listings can shift "unquantified risk" to less informed buyers, including retail investors, the ECB warned.
Government debt under strain
Shaky public finances in big advanced economies could also trigger a global repricing of government debt, the ECB warned. Long-term borrowing costs have hit their highest levels in more than two decades in several countries, and many eurozone governments are paying the most to borrow since the 2012 debt crisis.
Eurozone governments are issuing the most debt since the pandemic, driven mainly by Germany's defence and infrastructure spending.
With the ECB no longer buying government bonds under its stimulus programmes, more of it is going to foreign investors and hedge funds, which tend to be flightier in a crisis and could amplify any sell-off.
France stands out, with investors demanding more to cover political risk before the 2027 elections. Its 10-year borrowing costs topped 5% in October for the first time since 2002 and now stand at 4.85%.
On Tuesday, the Commission forecast EU public debt rising from 82.6% of GDP last year to 85.6% in 2028, with interest payments swallowing 2.4% of economic output by then.
"Fiscal consolidation is overdue," the ECB stated.
On the other hand, banks are in good shape to absorb shocks, the report said, with profitability at its highest in a decade and non-performing loans at a record low of 2.2% of the total in September.
Vulnerabilities are greater at some non-banks, such as investment funds and hedge funds, where safeguards are less developed. US tech and AI-related firms now make up between 16% and 26% of eurozone non-banks' equity investments.
The ECB pointed to the near-collapse in July of Situational Awareness, a US hedge fund whose assets under management shrank from around $45bn (€40.9bn) to $10bn (€9bn) after its leveraged AI bets went wrong.
Such stress could spread to banks, which get almost a fifth of their funding from non-banks. The ECB called for stronger safeguards against leverage and liquidity risks in the sector, while urging authorities to keep banks' capital buffers in place.
Higher energy prices could also leave households and companies struggling with repayments, and bad loans can take years to build up in the aftermath of an energy shock, the ECB warned.
The race to succeed Christine Lagarde
The report also lands as governments close in on a deal over the ECB's leadership.
Germany's finance ministry said on Tuesday it was seeking the chief economist job for Princeton University professor Markus Brunnermeier, with Berlin reportedly backing former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernández de Cos to replace Christine Lagarde as president in exchange.
The developments further indicate that France and Germany are nearing a deal to back the Spanish candidate, as Euronews reported last Friday.

noticias.titulo: Nearly 300,000 children abroad receive German benefits, sparking political backlash
noticias.resumen: New figures show that children of Polish nationals account for the largest share of Germany’s child benefit payments abroad, fuelling calls from some politicians to restrict payments to families living outside the country.
noticias.texto:
New figures show that children of Polish nationals account for the largest share of Germany’s child benefit payments abroad, fuelling calls from some politicians to restrict payments to families living outside the country.
Kindergeld is the German child benefit paid by the Familienkasse (German Family Benefits Office) to parents who work or are self-employed in Germany. In simple terms, it can be seen as the equivalent of Poland's 800+, since both benefits support families raising children and, under European Union rules, are treated as the same type of benefit.
In 2026 Kindergeld amounts to 259 euro per month for every child, that is around 1 140 zł.
The data requested from the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit - BA) by the Sojusz Sahry Wagenknecht (BSW), and first reported by "Bild", show that at the end of 2025 Kindergeld was being paid for 291 292 children living abroad. According to BA figures, this number almost tripled in 14 years: in 2011 there were 103 559 such children, and in 2015 there were 158 169.
Children living abroad account for about 1.66 percent of all 17.6 million children for whom Germany pays child benefit.
The figures show that for 112 384 of the 291 292 children living outside Germany, the parent entitled to receive Kindergeld is a Polish citizen. That is almost 39 percent of children living outside Germany. The second largest group is made up of 36 727 children of German citizens, which may include, for example, families where one parent works abroad. According to "Die Welt", next come citizens of the Czech Republic (33 872) and Romania (32 459).
Kindergeld paid into foreign bank accounts
According to the German portal Merkur.de, transfers of Kindergeld to foreign bank accounts have also clearly increased. In 2025 about 528 million euro was paid into such accounts, compared with just 45.7 million euro in 2011, more than eleven times less. However, these amounts cannot simply be equated with benefits for children living abroad. Kindergeld for such a child can be paid into a German account, while families with children in Germany can in turn use accounts abroad. The level of payments is also affected by increases in the benefit itself, so the rise in transfers does not allow the conclusion that the number of claimants has grown in proportion.
Why does Germany pay for children abroad?
Payments are based, among other things, on European rules on the coordination of social security benefits. Under these rules Germany may be the competent state for family benefits even when the child lives in another EU country. The right to Kindergeld stems from the parent working in Germany, not from where the child lives. A typical case is a parent working in Germany while the family still lives in the country of origin, for example Poland.
If several states are responsible for family benefits, priority rules apply which take account, among other things, of where the parents work and where the child lives. In certain circumstances Germany therefore pays not the full amount but only the difference compared with the lower benefit of the other state. A child living abroad does not therefore mean that the payment is unjustified. The statistics also do not show how often cross-border payments are abused.
Poles working in Germany can receive the benefit because the German child benefit is payable regardless of where the child lives. Receiving Poland's 800+ does not prevent the German benefit from being granted, but it has to be declared in the application. The application is submitted after working in Germany for at least four months.
German politicians are looking into the issue
German media report that politicians from the CDU/CSU and AfD are "deeply concerned" about the transfer of benefits from the German budget abroad. They acknowledge that the payments are for children of parents working in Germany, but point to the difference in living costs.
Günter Krings, deputy chair of the CDU/CSU group in the Bundestag, said that "Germany is the main exporter of child benefits to other EU countries".
He said: "The cost of living in Germany is significantly higher than in the countries where the children have remained. EU law currently forces us to pay the same child benefit for a child living abroad as for a child living in the country, provided the parents work here, completely ignoring the fact that the cost of living here is far higher than in many of those countries (...). The father works in Germany, his children live in Poland, Romania or the Czech Republic and receive German child benefit. Yet the current 259 euro per month for the first child is much less than, for example, in Timișoara. On average the cost of living in Romania is about 40 percent lower than in Germany".
The founder of BSW, Sahra Wagenknecht, goes furthest, calling for Kindergeld in principle no longer to be paid for children living outside Germany. In an interview with "Bild" she criticised the fact that the state transfers money abroad while people in Germany depend on food banks (Tafeln).
She wrote on X: "In Bitterfeld people are queuing up at food banks, and taxpayers' money is going to Bucharest. The German state is being plucked like a Christmas goose. Politicians need to think more about Bitterfeld again than about Bucharest. There must be no more benefits for children who do not live in Germany at all!"
AfD, for its part, has submitted a motion in the Bundestag to tie child benefit in EU countries to local living costs.
René Springer, a Bundestag member for AfD, said: "It is unfair that we are transferring child benefits at the full rate to foreign accounts. Romania pays 58 euro per child. We transfer 250 euro. Do these children really exist? Nobody checks that. For nine years we have been hearing that this is impossible. Now the issue has made it into an action plan, but only as a vague promise that we will one day ask the EU about it. The European Union will not represent our interests. We have to do that ourselves. When we are in government, we will reduce child benefits. And if the EU says this will not pass and sues us, we will simply pay less. We are the number one net contributor. This is a policy guided by the interests of German taxpayers".
CJEU: adjusting benefits is contrary to EU law
Such a rule is not easy to introduce at national level. European provisions on the coordination of family benefits oblige member states to recognise cross-border claims under certain conditions, so abolishing benefits across the board would require changes at European level.
Attempts have already been made to restrict the benefit. A few years ago the governing coalition announced a plan to limit Kindergeld for children living abroad, but this would have required amending EU rules, which prohibit such a move.
Austria provides an example. From 1 January 2019 Vienna adjusted benefits to the cost of living in the child's country of residence, and in June 2022 the Court of Justice of the EU found this to be incompatible with EU law (source in Polish). According to the Court, this amounted to indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality, without objective justification. The ruling was criticised by, among others, CDU MEP Daniel Caspary, who argued that Kindergeld is not part of remuneration but a state social benefit intended to support children where they live. In 2026 the Court also ruled that linking the Bavarian family allowance to the child's country of residence is contrary to EU law.
One percent of spending on children abroad
Parsa Marvi of the SPD took a different view. In an interview with "Die Welt" she recalled that equal treatment in relation to family benefits is an important element of the free movement of workers in the EU. She said: "Those who work here and help finance our society should not be discriminated against simply because of where their children live".
Janine Wissler, deputy chair of the Left party's parliamentary group, drew attention to the scale of the phenomenon: "We are talking about roughly one percent of total spending on child benefits".
The agency's figures show a similar proportion. In 2025 a total of 55.32 billion euro in Kindergeld was paid out, so the 528 million euro transferred to foreign accounts accounted for about 0.95 percent of all spending.

noticias.titulo: Von der Leyen proposes €45bn loan to Ukraine backed by joint debt
noticias.resumen: Brussels will go back to the markets to raise an additional €45 billion to keep Ukraine in the fight against Russia. Soaring borrowing costs are set to make the new credit costly and politically difficult.
noticias.texto:
Brussels will go back to the markets to raise an additional €45 billion to keep Ukraine in the fight against Russia. Soaring borrowing costs are set to make the new credit costly and politically difficult.
The European Commission has proposed issuing an additional €45 billion support loan to Ukraine, backed by joint debt, as the war-weary country fights to keep its economy afloat amid Russia's relentless airstrikes.
The loan, unveiled on Wednesday by President Ursula von der Leyen, envisages €20 billion for financial aid and €25 billion for weapons purchases such as drones, missiles and urgently needed air defence interceptors.
It will be disbursed gradually throughout 2027 and supplement the ongoing €90 billion loan, agreed by leaders in December last year.
"We are sending a clear message to Russia: We want peace," von der Leyen said.
"Five years since the start of this war of aggression, Europe stands united. We are as committed as ever to support Ukraine, in war and in peace."
Von der Leyen said she was "very confident" that all 27 member states, without exception, will back the proposal amid ongoing peace talks.
But four of them — Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria — have already made it clear they will not take part. Last year's fraught negotiations resulted in an opt-out for Bratislava, Prague and Budapest, which they now seek to continue.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has hit back, threatening to veto the next EU budget, including coveted cohesion funds, if fresh aid for Ukraine is not agreed by the 27 as a whole. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has called this "blackmail".
Von der Leyen sided with Merz and stressed the loan was split into two pillars, civilian and military, to assuage concerns of those who oppose weapon deliveries.
Leaders will have their first debate on the proposal next week when they meet in Brussels. The budget will also be on the table, providing a politically explosive mix.
Central to the debate will be the question of borrowing costs.
Though the Commission still enjoys a triple rating as a debt issuer, going to the markets to raise €45 billion will not come off cheap.
Interest rates have soared this year amid high energy prices, geopolitical volatility, investor jitters and the costly AI race. This means the bloc will have to foot billions in annual interest to keep the support going. Still, the prevailing opinion is that the costs of a failed Ukrainian state would exceed any financial undertaking.
As in previous operations, the repayment of the principal will be made contingent on Kyiv receiving war reparations. If Moscow, as expected, refuses to provide the compensation, Brussels reserves the right to use Russia's immobilised assets, worth €210 billion.
Kyiv is not expected to pay back out of pocket in any case.
"The option explicitly to use immobilised Russian cash balances to repay the support loan" is envisioned in the proposal, von der Leyen said.
"This is an additional point, I think, that shows that we cover the needs."
Standing alongside her, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said the draft EU budget, still under negotiation, will need to be re-examined to determine whether annual interest will be paid as part of or separately from future aid for Ukraine.
The €45 billion unveiled on Wednesday will come on top of the €90 billion support loan. That previous loan, which is still being disbursed, was designed under the assumption that Russia's war would end sometime in 2026.
The opposite has in fact happened: Moscow has escalated its attacks to make Ukraine's winter insufferable and destroy the levers of the local economy.
The non-stop barrage has disrupted business activity, hampered trade and triggered widespread blackouts, all of which diminish Kyiv's ability to collect revenue and maintain public services. This has made the country even more dependent on foreign aid.
The devastation has left a €70 billion shortfall in Ukraine's 2027 budget.
The bloc's new €45 billion loan is meant to cover two-thirds of this shortfall. The remaining third will fall on other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan.
Brussels will allow AAA-rated allies to chip in an additional €5 billion to the loan.

noticias.titulo: 'Human': Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2026 tackles ongoing AI fears
noticias.resumen: Amid the global and controversial debate surrounding artificial intelligence in daily life, Cambridge Dictionary has crowned “human” as its Word of the Year for 2026.
noticias.texto:
Amid the global and controversial debate surrounding artificial intelligence in daily life, Cambridge Dictionary has crowned “human” as its Word of the Year for 2026.
“Human” has been selected by Cambridge Dictionary as its 2026 Word of the Year.
It's a surprisingly familiar word, but one which reflects growing fears regarding AI and concerns linked to identity, creativity and what makes us unique in an increasingly AI-driven world.
Cambridge Dictionary's 2026 pick reflects the backlash to the divisive technology, as well as the ongoing debate over how artificial intelligence continues to blur the lines between machines and people.
“AI is changing how we talk about being human,” said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary’s lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children.”
The word, derived from the Latin “humanus”, is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
The dictionary cited public interventions by intellectuals such as AI pioneer and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, who said: “We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans."
"AI brings us back to questions that we've asked for millennia - who are we? What does it mean to be human?" said Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge. "AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There's a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."
Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.
“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to AI generating false or misleading information, and Merriam-Webster crowned "authentic".
Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its Word of the Year for low-quality content produced by AI, while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.
Other word contenders for Cambridge Dictionary's 2026 Word of the Year included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control, and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology. A non-tech contender this year was “wholesome”, a word to describe something which is likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.
Earlier this month, “mogging” was named Collins' Word of the Year, while Dictionary.com went for "maxxing" - both rather depressing terms which are being reclaimed by Gen Z in modern slang and conversation.

noticias.titulo: Bahrain sentences Shia clerics to life over alleged Iran plot amid torture allegations
noticias.resumen: Bahrain has arrested dozens of Shia clerics since the Iran war began in late February. Authorities accuse them of plotting with Tehran, while rights groups have raised concerns about torture and forced confessions. Gulf states have backed Bahrain’s judiciary.
noticias.texto:
Bahrain has arrested dozens of Shia clerics since the Iran war began in late February. Authorities accuse them of plotting with Tehran, while rights groups have raised concerns about torture and forced confessions. Gulf states have backed Bahrain’s judiciary.
A Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, most of whom are Shia clerics, to life in prison on Monday over an alleged Iran-backed plot to overthrow the government.
Five others received 15-year sentences, according to the UK-based Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD). The organisation said all 69 defendants were convicted, including 60 Shia clerics.
Among those sentenced to life was Sheikh Isa Qassim, a leading religious figure in Bahrain’s Shia community who lives in Iran, BIRD told Reuters. He was among 13 defendants tried in absentia.
Prosecutors said the defendants had formed and run a terrorist group linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). They accused members of raising money without authorisation and using mosques, sermons and charitable organisations to promote allegiance to Iran’s leadership.
The court also fined some defendants 100,000 Bahraini dinars (€240,000) and ordered the confiscation of more than 8 million dinars (€19.2 million) for charitable purposes, prosecutors said.
Before the verdict, 20 human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, had called for an independent investigation into torture allegations and urged the court to exclude any confessions obtained through abuse.
The groups said defendants had described prolonged blindfolding, sleep deprivation and threats against them and their families. Some said they had been questioned without lawyers and pressured into signing statements they were not allowed to read.
Defence lawyers were also prevented from obtaining copies of case files and had to rely on handwritten notes taken under tight time limits, the groups said.
Bahrain’s public prosecution said it respected defendants’ legal rights throughout the investigation and trial. It said lawyers representing those in custody had attended hearings and were able to examine evidence, question witnesses and present their arguments.
BIRD said the court brought the verdict forward from 22 November to Monday at prosecutors’ request. Defence lawyers were notified the evening before it was delivered.
The UK government said last Tuesday that it was aware of concerns about the trial and regularly discussed human rights, including fair trial guarantees, with Bahrain.
Iran condemns trial as Gulf states back Bahrain
Iran’s foreign ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday as a human rights violation and rejected allegations linking the defendants to Tehran.
Bahrain rejected the criticism, saying its courts judged criminal acts rather than religious beliefs and that the defendants had received the safeguards required by law.
On Wednesday, Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi expressed the bloc’s confidence in Bahrain’s judiciary and accused Iran of interfering in the country’s internal affairs.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, has faced Tehran's missile and drone attacks during the Iran war.
Authorities arrested dozens of Shia clerics and religious speakers in May and June, accusing them of seeking to overthrow the government with Iranian support.
Sunni and Shia are the two main branches of Islam, split in 632 over who should lead the Muslim community after the death of Prophet Muhammad.
Bahrain has a Shia-majority population, but it is ruled by a Sunni royal family.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine bets on flying evacuation drones to get wounded soldiers out of 'kill zone'
noticias.resumen: The Stargate drone can travel at 105 kilometres per hour, carry loads of up to 150 kilograms with a range of 30 kilometres. Each one costs about €45,000.
noticias.texto:
The Stargate drone can travel at 105 kilometres per hour, carry loads of up to 150 kilograms with a range of 30 kilometres. Each one costs about €45,000.
Ukrainian soldier Yevgen had been stuck on the front line for two days, his foot torn off by a mine.
Just as he was losing hope, a comrade told him salvation was coming from above: a flying evacuation drone.
"I said, 'you're kidding, right? You're just trying to cheer me up'," he told the AFP news agency.
Now recovering in a hospital bed, Yevgen, whose surname cannot be disclosed for security reasons, was one of the first Ukrainians to be evacuated by an aerial medical drone.
Almost five years after Russia invaded, drones have transformed the very nature of modern warfare.
They dominate the skies, with the front line now known as a "kill zone" several kilometres deep. There, both sides can send explosive-packed machines crashing down at the slightest sign of movement below.
That has made rescuing wounded soldiers caught inside the kill zone almost impossible for ground forces and combat medics.
Instead, Ukrainian drone producers have turned their hand to evacuation craft. The one that saved Yevgen, called Stargate and developed by manufacturer Skyfall, has been used in three missions.
"Later in the evening the company commander called me and said: 'Well, are you ready to fly?'," said Yevgen.
Footage from the drone's camera shows him taking his place in the pod, a flying stretcher then covered with a lid, in the dark of night as he clutched a gun to his chest.
As he was flown back, supply and surveillance drones buzzed below and above him, their silhouettes cast against the night moon.
Despite his fear, "there was no other option", he said.
Secret location
The carbon-fibre drones are assembled in a secret hangar that resembles a laboratory.
The idea of an evacuation drone came from a request of the commander of Ukraine's CODE 9.2 assault brigade.
"A year later, we had the Stargate," a Skyfall representative told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.
It was born from "operational need" rather than any new technological breakthrough.
Ukraine had previously been using ground drones to evacuate its wounded from dangerous positions. But they can only travel at 10 kilometres per hour and struggle to cross rivers, minefields and other tricky terrain.
"They are also easy targets," the company spokesperson added. "A mission can last several hours."
Stargate can travel at 105 kilometres per hour, carry loads of up to 150 kilograms with a range of 30 kilometres. Each one costs about $50,000 (€45,000).
In the workshop, several were lined up along a central aisle. Behind them, the metal frames of prototypes collect dust.
Skyfall aims to produce 1,000 per month by the end of 2026.
Outside the factory, a test flight: the 400-kilogram machine rose into the air with a roar resembling an imminent thunderstorm.
Behind the controls were trainee pilots. Until now, they had only navigated drones carrying supplies or bombs.
'Library silence'
"As soon as I picked him up everyone went quiet," the drone pilot who rescued Yevgen told AFP.
"There was just silence, library silence," the pilot, known by his call sign of "KVN", added. "This time there was a person on board."
Before take-off, several Russian attack drones were spotted, forcing a suspension. A second attempt was also aborted.
The third time around, the drone finally took off, climbing to an altitude of 100 metres.
Russian electronic jammers briefly cut KVN's link with the drone, a nerve-wracking moment as it hovered for a while in the middle of the aerial battlefield.
After a few seconds, the on-board artificial intelligence took over, until the connection was restored.
The whole evacuation took about 15 minutes and was closely monitored by a team of Ukrainian troops.
The army is cautiously optimistic about the technology.
"We need more examples in the field to really assess the system (but) it looks promising," said one officer, speaking on condition of anonymity.
For KVN, the drones represent "a future, driven by technology, that will bring soldiers back to their families".
Yevgen is a preacher now, trying to convert his fellow comrades who are "afraid".
"I send them messages to explain that they have nothing to fear."

noticias.titulo: Early alerts, simple journeys and a stress-free experience: What passengers want at airports
noticias.resumen: ACI World’s 2027 global traveller survey found that while 77% of passengers leave airports with ‘positive emotions’, they are seeking seamless journeys and want to be kept in the loop about potential disruptions.
noticias.texto:
ACI World’s 2027 global traveller survey found that while 77% of passengers leave airports with ‘positive emotions’, they are seeking seamless journeys and want to be kept in the loop about potential disruptions.
More travellers are enjoying their time at airports, according to a new industry report.
In the 2027 Global Traveller Survey published by Airports Council International (ACI) World and conducted in collaboration with research company Potloc, a total of 4,125 respondents from 30 countries were asked about their airport experience.
According to the survey, which polled travellers who had flown at least once in the 12 months preceding August 2026, 77% said their airport journeys left them with “positive emotions”. This marks an increase from 73% and 69% in 2025 and 2024, respectively.
Further, 67% of travellers described the airport as a “comfortable and relaxing” place.
“More travellers are leaving airports feeling good,” Justin Erbacci, ACI World Director General, said. “That is the result of airports putting passengers first, every single day.
“Travellers know some disruption will always be part of travel. When it happens, keeping them informed and in control makes all the difference.”
What travellers want at an airport
Despite global travel in 2026 being marked by disruptions including heatwaves and airspace closures, the report’s findings point to a “more positive picture” beyond the headlines, while also showing what travellers want next.
The research found that respondents want to be “kept in the loop” in instances where plans change. Steps, such as early alerts about potential disruption, were the personalised support travellers valued the most (48%). "Information that arrives before the problem does help them stay in control of their journey," the report said.
They also like things kept simple. According to the findings, a smooth journey is marked by “how it feels”, and not necessarily the “technology behind it”. Examples include lower waiting times alongside easy navigation and predictable journey times, with 64% of respondents describing airports as “seamless”.
Lastly, “calm comes first”, the report said. Stress-free, relaxed experiences are top priorities for travellers between security and boarding processes. “A smooth journey gives them that time back, and airports are making the most of it, with thoughtfully designed dining, art, activities and shops.” Nine in 10 travellers say airport shopping makes their experience better.
“ACI advocates for airports, airlines and governments to work as one system,” Erbacci said. “We each hold a piece of the journey, but the passenger experiences only one. When the journey flows, airports become places to enjoy, not just pass through.”

noticias.titulo: Drug that mimics Viagra shows promise as Alzheimer's treatment
noticias.resumen: Experts said the results are encouraging, but that more research is needed before the drug is offered to patients.
noticias.texto:
Experts said the results are encouraging, but that more research is needed before the drug is offered to patients.
An experimental drug that mimics Viagra could help slow down Alzheimer’s disease, a new global study has found.
The drug, called AR1001, is taken as a once-daily tablet. In a late-stage clinical trial, AR1001 slowed cognitive decline and memory loss by 31% among 604 people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not taking other treatments.
The results were not statistically significant in a wider group of Alzheimer’s patients who also took other drugs, according to AriBio, the South Korean company that makes AR1001.
Experts said the results are encouraging, but that more research is needed before AR1001 is offered to patients.
“These topline results are an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms,” said Richard Oakley, associate director for research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society.
Like the erectile dysfunction drug Viagra, AR1001 belongs to a class of drugs called PDE5 inhibitors. AR1001 works by relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain — though Oakley cautioned against taking Viagra to try to treat Alzheimer’s.
“AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said.
In the trial, which took place in 13 countries, most side effects were mild to moderate, including diarrhoea, falls and dizziness, AriBio said.
The study results were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in the United States. AriBio said it plans to discuss the findings with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, which affects 57 million people worldwide. There is currently no cure, prompting researchers to search for treatments to slow the progression of the disease.
“We look forward to seeing the full results from this trial and how this drug progresses,” Oakley said.

noticias.titulo: Amazon's Jeff Bezos, RFK Jr and Hollywood celebrities comment on Robert Pattinson casting as James Bond
noticias.resumen: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.” From Amazon boss Jeff Bezos to Brad Pitt via some of Robert Pattinson's former co-stars, here's the lowdown on the reactions to the seventh 007.
noticias.texto:
“Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.” From Amazon boss Jeff Bezos to Brad Pitt via some of Robert Pattinson's former co-stars, here's the lowdown on the reactions to the seventh 007.
The rumour circus is over now that Robert Pattinson has been officially cast the seventh James Bond – a role the actor called the “honour of a lifetime” and “a dream come true”.
While reactions have been mixed – if broadly positive – it has now been revealed that Amazon boss Jeff Bezos had a role in the casting.
Speaking at an event in California, Bezos told the audience he was “heavily involved” in the casting process. He shared why Pattinson was cast despite some concern that the British actor is already famous – thereby breaking the unwritten rule that Bond must be played by and up-and-coming actor.
“Initially, I’d say we were slightly biased a little against him because he’s already so famous,” Bezos said. “We sort of thought, maybe we should have someone a little more unknown.”
He continued: “But in the screening test, it’s so obvious. He is James Bond."
Bezos added that the final five actors selected for the next 007 were “extraordinarily talented” but that there was "something special about Rob.”
Pattinson's Bond debut will be the first released since Amazon’s acquisition of MGM, the Hollywood studio behind the famous franchise.
His casting has drawn high praise from those inside (and outside) the entertainment industry.
The royal family shared news of the casting to their official Instagram page, writing: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond”, while a spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the PM is "obviously delighted for Robert Pattinson" and that the role was "an amazing opportunity.”
Across the pond, Donald Trump's health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr decided it was a good idea to join in and shared – surprise, surprise – an AI-generated image of him as 007, swapping out a gun for a giant carrot and captioning the post: “Food. Real Food.”
The internet was swift in mocking the post and bemoaning the fact that Trump's cabinet are the least serious people around. “Who voted for this shit?” read one comment, while another posted: “America needs food safety, not a Cabinet secretary auditioning for Veggie Bond”.
On a significantly more serious note, Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve said in an interview with GQ that the most important qualities he was looking for in the search for his 007.
The Oscar-nominated Canadian filmmaker behind Prisoners, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049 and the Dune films said: “The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin. I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that.”
He continued: “I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to… someone who has dark humor, someone that has pleasure in being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud. “I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us.”
Clearly Pattinson checked off all the boxes.
Villeneuve previously worked with Pattinson on the yet-to-be-released Dune: Part Three.
Elsewhere, various celebrities have praised Pattinson's casting.
Rami Malek, who played villain Safin in Daniel Craig's swansong adventure No Time to Die, said Pattinson will be “extraordinary” as 007.
Speaking at the Earthshot Awards in Mumbai, he said: “I have known Rob for quite some time, and I could not be more proud. The fact that people are recognising, I think, maybe they all know, how talented that man is.”
Ralph Fiennes, who played M in Skyfall, Spectre and No Time To Die (and who killed Pattinson in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire), said during an interview with Andy Cohen on SiriusXM Front Row: "I’m sorry. I’m in love with Daniel Craig still,” before adding that he believes Pattinson is up to the task. “No, he’s a great actor,” he said. “I’m sure he’ll be great.”
Pattinson's Tenet co-star Elizabeth Debicki said she was “so thrilled” for the actor who, according to her, will be “the perfect Bond”.
“He is an enigma himself. He’s beautiful, and he’s funny, and he’s smart… I think he’s perfect. I’m so thrilled,’” she said as per Variety, adding that “he’s evolved so much as an actor. He’s made really interesting choices. He’s really smart”.
Hollywood star Brad Pitt also publicly backed Pattinson’s appointment, telling red carpet reporters: “I love this idea. I love what he’s been doing. I love his choices, and I think he’s the real deal. That’s great. Good call.” Pitt also cheekily added that he wouldn't be against the idea of playing a future Bond baddie in one of Pattinson's films.
As for the previous Bonds, George Lazenby, the oldest living 007 actor, has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the fold.
The 87-year-old, who played Bond once in 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, posted a video message on Instagram welcoming Pattinson into the club.
“Robert, welcome to the most exclusive club in the world,” Lazenby said, before offering up advice: “But remember to enjoy yourself. Let’s see if you’ll have a ‘this never happened to the other fella’ moment.” Lazenby concluded: “All the best mate, George.”
Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond on the big screen – Sean Connery, Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.
As for the release of the yet-untitled Bond 26, audiences will have to wait a little longer.
Production is expected to start next year, but Pattinson will have to complete filming The Batman Part II – production on which was temporarily paused after director Matt Reeves was faced with a personal issue. Steven Soderbergh has stepped in to help shoot the final few weeks.
This means that the earliest we'll get to see the next Bond adventure will be in the second half of 2028 - making it seven years since No Time To Die and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

noticias.titulo: Huge plume of gas erupts from Los Angeles landfill after drilling accident
noticias.resumen: Six people were taken to hospital with minor injuries after drilling at a landfill in Los Angeles County triggered a sudden release of gas and decomposing waste. The incident sent a large plume high into the air, prompting warnings for nearby residents.
noticias.texto:
Six people were taken to hospital with minor injuries after a drilling operation at a landfill in Los Angeles County triggered a sudden release of gas and decomposing waste.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The incident happened on Monday at the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in Castaic, where crews were carrying out routine drilling around 46 metres below ground.
Workers struck naturally occurring landfill gas produced by decomposing rubbish, causing it to escape through the drilling hole. The gas carried small pieces of decomposing waste into the air, creating a large cloud, according to fire department officials.
The city of Santa Clarita urged the public to avoid the area and advised some nearby residents to be prepared to evacuate.

noticias.titulo: Cheers and reactions in Alaska after Mary Peltola's Senate win
noticias.resumen: Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska's closely fought Senate race, securing a political comeback in a state that has repeatedly backed Donald Trump.
noticias.texto:
Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, completing a political comeback in a state where President Donald Trump has won by wide margins.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The result makes Alaska the last Senate race to be decided in the 2026 US midterm elections and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the chamber, after flipping nine Republican-held seats.
Peltola's victory was welcomed by supporters across Alaska, particularly members of Native communities, who say she understands the difficulties of living in remote villages, including the high cost of living.

noticias.titulo: Dubai's businesses gain an AI workforce on demand
noticias.resumen: Dubai launches Chamber AI Hub, the first chamber-led agentic AI marketplace, with ready-made agents and training to help companies transform operations.
noticias.texto:
Ready-made AI agents, available to try and hire through Dubai Chambers, and new training partnerships with Nebius Academy and Lovable put Dubai's companies at the front of the shift to agentic AI.
“Success in the transition to Agentic AI is measured not by technology adoption alone, but by how effectively companies use these tools to address business challenges and deliver tangible results.”
Those were the words of H.E. Eng. Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, Chairman of Dubai Chambers, as the organisation launched Chamber AI Hub, the world's first chamber-led agentic AI marketplace, on 26 October.
The hub gives companies operating in Dubai access to ready-to-use, specialised AI agents that can carry out a wide range of administrative and operational tasks. A week earlier, Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy signed two agreements with international AI companies to equip businesses with the skills to use them.
Both moves deliver on the directives of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the UAE, and Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai, to accelerate the adoption of agentic AI across Dubai's private sector, a programme overseen by Dubai Chambers.
Ready-made agents for everyday business
Chamber AI Hub opens with 22 specialised AI agents across seven business functions: compliance, procurement, operations, finance, sales, human resources and logistics. The catalogue is set to grow to 100 agents over two years.
Each agent is designed for a specific job. Between them they can find suppliers and evaluate vendor proposals, monitor supply chain risks, review contracts, match invoices against purchase orders, generate business proposals, screen CVs, score sales leads and handle IT help desk requests.
Dubai Chambers members choose the agents most relevant to their business and subscribe to packages offered with competitive benefits.
Try before you buy
The hub has been built to make adoption simple and low risk. Companies can try any agent in a sandbox before activating it, and receive complimentary credits to get started before moving to paid packages based on usage.
A readiness assessment helps businesses judge their preparedness, while dashboards show usage levels and costs and the platform reports each agent's success rate in fulfilling requests. A company admin portal allows managers to oversee how their teams use AI agents.
The platform complies with all relevant UAE regulatory requirements and data protection standards. Data is hosted in the UAE, each company's information is kept separate, and every agent supports both Arabic and English.
Al Mansoori said the hub reflects Dubai Chambers' focus on turning knowledge into results.
“This is why we are connecting knowledge with practical application, building capabilities, and expanding access to specialised solutions and high-quality tools that help companies adapt to change and evolve the way they work,” he said.
“Through this approach, we are preparing a private sector that is equipped to respond to technological transformation and contribute to shaping the opportunities of the future economy.”
'The right skills and capabilities'
Alongside the tools comes the training. On 19 October, in the presence of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, one of the three chambers operating under Dubai Chambers, signed two memorandums of understanding to accelerate agentic AI adoption across the private sector.
“We are committed to strengthening the ability of Dubai-based companies to understand and effectively adopt Agentic AI technologies, supporting their digital ambitions, creating new opportunities for growth and enhancing their competitiveness,” said Saeed Al Gergawi, Vice President of Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy.
“Through these collaborations, we aim to build a more innovative, agile and future-ready business community by providing access to specialised knowledge and expertise.”
The first agreement is with Nebius Academy, the education and training arm of AI cloud company Nebius, which has a market capitalisation of more than US$63 billion. It will deliver specialised training in AI leadership and agentic AI through Dubai Chambers Academy, including training content, certifications, technical workshops and expert-led sessions for executives, technical teams and employees of Dubai Chamber of Commerce member companies.
“Through our collaboration with Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, Nebius Academy will equip businesses across Dubai with the practical knowledge needed to move from understanding Agentic AI to applying it effectively in their daily operations,” said Raja Agrawal, Vice President for the Middle East and Africa at Nebius.
“Agentic AI has the potential to transform how companies operate, innovate and grow. However, realising this potential requires more than access to technology. It also requires the right skills and capabilities. We are proud to support Dubai’s ambition to build a future-ready private sector and develop the AI capabilities that will drive the next generation of business innovation.”
'Anyone with an idea'
The second agreement, with software creation platform Lovable, is aimed at founders and entrepreneurs. Lovable will provide access to its platform and educational resources, take part in joint events and workshops, and supply platform credits, funded by Dubai Chambers, to participants in the Create AI Agents Championship.
“Agentic AI enables anyone with an idea to bring it to life,” said Lauren Rhode, Head of Revenue at Lovable.
“We are pleased to support more founders and businesses in Dubai by providing the tools they need to launch and operate their solutions, starting with the teams participating in the Create AI Agents Championship.”
Together with the hub, the agreements serve both sides of the market: the companies adopting AI agents and the founders building them.
A city moving as one
Both initiatives sit within a two-year programme that aims to enable more than 295,000 private sector companies in Dubai, supported by specialised training tracks for 14,000 member companies of the Business Groups and Business Councils operating under Dubai Chamber of Commerce.
Some of the emirate's best-known companies are already on board. Also in October, in the presence of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed, 11 Dubai-based companies pledged to integrate agentic AI into their operations: Emirates, DP World, AW Rostamani Group, Al Ansari Exchange, Dubai Islamic Bank, Kitopi, Dutco Group, Aster DM Healthcare, Innovo, Independent Food Company and HSA Group.
In most economies, companies are left to find, test, buy and learn to use AI agents on their own. Dubai has brought all of it together under its chamber of commerce, giving businesses of every size a single, trusted route in, and giving international AI developers a market ready to adopt their solutions.
With the hub's catalogue set to grow from 22 to 100 agents and training rolling out across thousands of member companies, Dubai's private sector is moving from trial to everyday use of agentic AI.
Companies can explore the platform at aihub.dubaichambers.com.

noticias.titulo: Xi and Putin meet ahead of planned summit with Trump
noticias.resumen: Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen ahead of a rare trilateral summit with Donald Trump, focusing on energy, finance and global security.
noticias.texto:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026, ahead of a planned trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering, with discussions expected to cover energy, finance and foreign policy, including Ukraine and North Korea.
