noticias.titulo: Carney backs Trump’s nuclear talks with Xi and Putin
noticias.resumen: Canada's prime minister also blasted the Russian president over his war in Ukraine.
noticias.texto: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday gave cautious backing to U.S. President Donald Trump’s planned three-way meeting with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Speaking to reporters at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, Carney welcomed the trilateral meeting’s focus on nuclear arms control . “I’m going to say something positive here about the initiative around denuclearization,” he said, adding that “Canada is in favor of denuclearization.” The first trilateral meeting between the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders is set to take place Thursday on the sidelines of the summit. The White House has said Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms and the war with Iran. Ukraine is not expected to be on the agenda. Trump told reporters last week that the leaders would “talk a lot of things, including denuclearization.” Carney’s partial endorsement of the trilateral meeting comes amid ongoing friction with Washington over trade. He said the U.S. had “fundamentally changed its trading objectives,” describing the talks as a “two steps forward, one step back type thing.” He is due to meet Trump later Wednesday. Carney had stern words for Putin, who said in a speech at the APEC CEO Summit that sanctions are “a thing of the past,” adding that “while they may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth.” Asked to comment on the remarks, Carney said the Russian president “can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past.” Carney also accused the Kremlin chief of misrepresenting the war in Ukraine. “Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground,” he added.

noticias.titulo: Deadly drug-resistant infections are surging in European hospitals
noticias.resumen: Strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae have evolved to resist even the newest antibiotics.
noticias.texto: A dangerous drug-resistant superbug is surging in European hospitals, spreading between patients and becoming increasingly harder to treat, the EU’s disease agency warns. Cases of bloodstream infections caused by treatment-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae have increased by 72% between 2019 and 2025 — way off a target of cutting rates by 5% by 2030 — according to the latest bundle of reports from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, out Wednesday. Infections linked to this bacterium, which have been climbing steadily for the past few years , are a significant threat to patients in hospitals and have a high mortality rate typically between 40% and 70%. Analyses show that several of its strains are becoming resistant to nearly all antibiotics — including new ones — and can cause severe illness and death. The findings on treatment-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae were “the biggest concern” among all the data collected on superbugs in Europe over the past year, Christian Giske, who leads this work at ECDC, told a press briefing. It’s one example of the dangers posed by antimicrobial resistance — the ability of bacteria and fungi to evolve to be resistant to drugs designed to destroy them — which is estimated to kill 35,000 people in the EU, Iceland and Norway every year. For Europe, this is a “major public health threat,” Giske said. Despite progress in some areas, the latest reports show the EU is still far from reaching its 2030 targets to reduce rates of drug-resistant infections. Among the challenges is the limited number of new drugs available to treat such infections. The news comes as Europe’s new pharmaceutical legislation is set to be signed into law in December and includes measures to boost the discovery and development of new antibiotics — through a market monopoly perk for industry and a push for steady payment models for countries to buy them. Harder to tackle Given that it spreads between patients, tackling the surging rates of Klebsiella requires stronger infection prevention and control measures in hospitals, the ECDC warns. This includes strengthening hand hygiene, ensuring correct use of personal protective equipment like gloves, and effective environmental cleaning and disinfection. And while similar measures have helped to significantly cut EU rates of the better-known hospital-acquired superbug, MRSA, for Klebsiella, missing even the tiniest surface can lead to the bacteria spreading. “Klebsiella is a gut bacterium, and it may have more powerful reservoirs in the body,” Giske told reporters during the press briefing. “What works for MRSA might not be sufficient for Klebsiella. The adherence to good [infection prevention and control] needs to be even higher to contain a problem like Klebsiella.” Countries have successfully fought back against infections with MRSA — otherwise known as drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: In 2025, bloodstream infections caused by this bacterium were 19% lower than in 2019, surpassing the target of reducing them by 15% by 2030. While countries have been successfully using infection control measures to drive down rates of MRSA, Klebsiella is harder to tackle, said Giske. E. coli drug-resistant infections are also proving difficult to drive down: Despite a target to reduce these infections by 10% by 2030, the EU saw a 16.4% increase between 2019 and 2025. Mixed progress It’s also key to ensure reduced and targeted use of antibiotics, as avoiding antibiotics when they are not needed can reduce the risk of bacteria becoming resistant to them. New estimates show that antibiotic consumption in the EU dropped by 5% between 2019 and 2025, well below the 20% target by 2030. Meanwhile, the EU is slowly making progress in using the right types of antibiotics. It’s inching closer to its goal of ensuring that at least 65% of antibiotics being used in Europe are the correct drugs — as determined by the World Health Organization — with the proportion reaching 62.5% in 2025. “We are still behind with several of the EU’s 2030 targets to counter antimicrobial resistance,” ECDC Director Pamela Rendi-Wagner said in a statement. Genomic surveillance is one recent innovation making a difference. This helps authorities to assess more quickly how these resistant bacteria are spreading, Rendi-Wagner said. “This in turn means we can act sooner to stop transmission, more effectively guide treatment decisions, and identify where new antibiotics are most urgently needed,” she added.

noticias.titulo: Procès “femmeblancherie” : quand l’idéologie masculiniste devient une menace sécuritaire
noticias.resumen: Des associations de lutte contre la haine en ligne veulent faire de ce procès un exemple des dangers du masculinisme pour la sécurité nationale.
noticias.texto: PARIS — Ils sont infirmiers, agents pénitentiaires ou conducteurs de métro. Au fil des mois, ces hommes ont échangé, entre deux pauses café ou sur le chemin du travail, des messages haineux et des appels à la violence contre des femmes sur un canal Telegram public, nommé “femmeblancherie” et comptant 1 758 abonnés. Ce mercredi 18 novembre s’ouvre le procès de plusieurs de ses membres au tribunal judiciaire de Paris, à l’issue d’une enquête confiée à l’Office central de lutte contre les crimes contre l’humanité et les crimes de haine (OCLCH) et révélée début août par Le Figaro . Les prévenus, dont l’administrateur du canal, risquent en moyenne un an d’emprisonnement et 45 000 euros d’amende pour plusieurs délits, dont “provocation publique à la haine ou à la violence envers une personne ou un groupe de personnes en raison du sexe”. Interrogé par POLITICO, le parquet de Paris note aussi “de nombreux propos à caractère racial, des apologies du terrorisme et de crime contre l’humanité”. En face, les associations de lutte contre la haine en ligne, comme Point de contact, StopFisha, Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement et la Fondation des femmes, se sont constituées parties civiles au procès. Leur objectif : l’ériger en exemple des dangers du masculinisme pour la sécurité nationale. “Ce qui n’est pas assez identifié, c’est le lien entre les masculinistes et le passage à l’acte violent”, explique à POLITICO Alejandra Mariscal, directrice de Point de contact. “Telegram est la partie émergée de l’iceberg, il faut évoquer la porosité avec les autres services numériques et le continuum entre les violences en ligne et hors ligne.” Il faut dire que les affaires du genre se multiplient. Questionné par POLITICO, le Parquet national antiterroriste (Pnat) pointe l’essor, en 2025, des enquêtes sur “ce champ idéologique protéiforme” — qui reste toutefois marginal par rapport à d’autres menaces, comme les courants djihadistes. La toute première enquête a ainsi été ouverte en juin 2025, soit quelques mois avant le début des investigations sur le réseau “femmeblancherie”. Elle concernait un jeune homme de 18 ans se revendiquant de la mouvance Incel, rappelle le Pnat à POLITICO. L’épineux problème des “zones grises” L’administrateur du groupe “femmeblancherie” postait quotidiennement des publications sur la thématique du “problème femme”, largement commentées par ses abonnés. L’enquête a aussi mis en avant l’attrait des membres pour les mouvances d’extrême droite radicales. L’exploitation des téléphones des prévenus a ainsi révélé une appétence des abonnés du canal pour les sites des négationnistes Alain Soral et de Vincent Reynouard, “eux-mêmes fréquemment condamnés pour des incitations à la haine”, souligne le parquet de Paris, qui précise que Telegram a répondu à toutes les réquisitions et permis d’identifier un certain nombre de prévenus. Ces derniers ont reconnu pour la plupart les messages, mais se défendent en invoquant “un ‘humour noir’ ou ‘humour beauf’, ou avoir écrit sous l’effet de l’alcool ou de l’agacement”, relate le parquet. L’argument de l’humour est justement au cœur des difficultés rencontrées par les associations lorsqu’elles souhaitent obtenir un retrait de contenus par les plateformes, témoignent-elles. Car ces “contenus gris” ne sont pas complètement répréhensibles et peu encadrés par les conditions générales d’utilisation des réseaux sociaux, bien qu’ils participent à la diffusion de ce courant de pensée. “Il peut s’agir de vidéos d’influenceurs, y compris avec une petite audience, sur les rapports homme/femme, la ‘place’ de la femme dans la société ou le sujet du body count [le nombre de partenaires sexuels, NDLR]”, illustre Alejandra Mariscal, qui s’inquiète de leur diffusion auprès d’un public mineur. “Ces contenus gris ne sont pas considérés comme préjudiciables et notre rôle de signaleur de confiance est donc limité. Il faut réussir à les intégrer dans la définition d’un contenu illicite et c’est ce à quoi nous travaillons avec l’Observatoire de la haine en ligne, piloté par l’Arcom”, abonde auprès de POLITICO Véronique Béchu, directrice de l’Observatoire contre le harcèlement et les violences numériques faites aux mineurs au sein de l’association e-Enfance. Et après ? Au-delà du procès, qui doit durer jusqu’en janvier, l’enjeu pour les associations est d’élargir le champ des contenus illicites à certains propos sexistes, et de renforcer la responsabilité des plateformes en les considérant de moins en moins comme de simples hébergeurs de contenu. Une piste qu’ont explorée les sénatrices Olivia Richard (UCI), Béatrice Gosselin (LR) et Laurence Rossignol (PS) dans un vaste rapport sur le sujet . Les trois élues y proposent de préciser la notion de “risque systémique” que doivent prévenir les plateformes dans le cadre du règlement européen sur les services numériques (DSA) pour y intégrer les propos masculinistes. L’Arcom n’est pas en reste : l’autorité a remis, en mars, un rapport sur “le sexisme sur les plateformes en ligne” avec des recommandations similaires. Le régulateur y encourage les plateformes et la communauté scientifique à qualifier les contenus relevant de cette “zone grise”, et à évaluer leurs effets sur les publics. Il appelle aussi les plateformes à renforcer la transparence de leur système de recommandation et à coopérer davantage avec les autorités publiques.

noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Während der Kanzler die Koalition der Willigen morgen zur Ukraine-Unterstützung in Berlin versammelt, inszeniert sich Donald Trump heute schon am anderen Ende der Welt. Beim Gipfel im chinesischen Shenzhen trifft er auf Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin, während seine Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner im Kanzleramt weitgehend schweigen müssen. Was dieses geopolitische Schattenspiel für den Westen bedeutet, analysiert Vize-Chefredakteurin Annett Meiritz zusammen mit Rixa Fürsen. Wie blickt Europa auf dieses Dreiertreffen der Weltmächte, bei dem die EU nicht dabei ist? Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, Vorsitzende des EU-Verteidigungsausschusses, erklärt im 200-Sekunden-Interview, warum es paradoxerweise ein gutes Zeichen ist, dass in China nicht über die Ukraine gesprochen wird und welche Rolle der Iran in Trumps globalem Machtpoker spielt. Nach elf Jahren hat die Bundeswehr ihren Einsatz im Irak beendet, auch die US-Truppen sind abgezogen. Nun reist Entwicklungsministerin Reem Alabali Radovan nach Erbil, um den Fokus auf wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit zu lenken. POLITICO-Reporterin Carlotta Diederich berichtet vor Ort, wie fragil die Sicherheitslage im irakischen Machtvakuum zwischen IS-Überresten und pro-iranischen Milizen tatsächlich ist. Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig. Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren. noticias.titulo: Listen: Are EU sanctions against Russia really affecting the war effort?
noticias.resumen: The EU is preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia. It is expected before the end of the year. This time, the measures are set to target more banks and crypto assets, as well as more ships from the so-called shadow fleet, those cargo that transport Russian oil, often under false flags. So, are those sanctions actually putting pressure on Russia?
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : The EU is preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia. It is expected before the end of the year. This time, the measures are set to target more banks and crypto assets, as well as more ships from the so-called shadow fleet, those cargo that transport Russian oil, often under false flags. So, are those sanctions actually putting pressure on Russia? First, a quick reminder of what these sanctions have achieved so far. The EU has blacklisted more than 2,700 individuals and entities, and frozen over 200 billion euros in Russian assets held in the EU. Not to mention the numerous trade restrictions, starting with oil and gas. Now the big question is: does it really impact Russia’s economy: yes it does, at least to a certain extent. European imports of Russian goods have fallen dramatically since 2022, by around three quarters. The EU has also almost completely stopped importing Russian oil and gas. Read more Europe’s mandate on Russia-Ukraine peace talks takes shape, as Putin escalates war Now Russia is not feeling as much pain as European policymakers would have hoped. Take the restrictions on exports of high-tech products and so-called dual-use goods, which can serve both civilian and military purposes. Russia can no longer buy many of these products directly from European suppliers. But it has found alternative sources, particularly in China. According to a report published last week by the European Court of Auditors, these alternative supply routes come at a higher cost for Russia. The same goes for oil and gas. Moscow has managed to redirect much of the energy it used to sell to Europe towards Asian markets. Gas is more difficult to reroute than oil, though. It requires either liquefaction facilities and specialised ships, or pipelines connecting Russia to new markets. And those infrastructures are not available everywhere. So, how is the Russian economy actually holding up? Read more EU flexes muscle on Russia sanctions, as Trump and Putin discuss Ukraine’s future in China Well, it’s under pressure, but it’s far from collapsing. According to a report published last year by the Centre for Eastern Studies, Russia is not on the brink of a major economic crisis, despite the sanctions. So how is Moscow managing to finance its war without bringing its economy to its knees? There are several factors. First, oil and gas revenues remain an important source of income for the Russian state. Second, Russia has massively expanded its defence industry. This boosts economic activity and contributes to GDP growth, while also supplying the war effort. But this comes at a cost. Military spending puts considerable pressure on public finances, forcing the government to raise taxes, including VAT. And the effects are not felt equally across the economy. Many businesses outside the defence sector are struggling, while wages are coming under pressure. Combined with higher taxes, this means that ordinary Russians are also feeling the economic consequences of the war. Read more Watchdog finds patchy customs controls leave big loopholes in EU’s Russia trade sanctions Finally, are there still levers the EU could use to put more pressure on Russia Some argue that most of the available options have already been exhausted. But others point out that there are still areas where the EU could take action – and hasn’t. According to the European Court of Auditors, one area where there is still room for improvement is enforcement. Auditors found that sanctions were not being applied consistently across customs authorities, creating loopholes that Russia is able to exploit. Then, there are potential new sanctions that Europeans could adopt: one example is maritime services. European companies still provide services to Russian ships, including insurance, shipbroking and assistance. But three EU member states – Greece, Malta and Cyprus – have opposed sanctions targeting these services, partly because of the importance of their maritime industries. Other economic sectors remain untouched because of disagreements among the 27 member states. So, while the sanctions have significantly reduced Russia’s economic ties with Europe and made some imports more expensive, they have not stopped Moscow from finding alternative suppliers or financing its war effort. This does not mean that it has no impact. Far from it. What this says is that the fight goes hand in hand with the active support for Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: Was this a modern Gleiwitz? Poland’s sources allege a Russian false-flag plot near Kaliningrad
noticias.resumen: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported on Wednesday that security forces prevented a suspected Russian intelligence operation ...
noticias.texto: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported on Wednesday that security forces prevented a suspected Russian intelligence operation near the border with the Kaliningrad exclave in late October and early November. Citing senior security sources, the paper described an alleged plan involving sabotage on Polish territory combined with a possible staged attack that could be attributed to Ukraine, with the intent of producing significant casualties and planting evidence to implicate Kyiv. One source compared the concept to the 1939 Gleiwitz incident, a Nazi false-flag operation (also known as Operation Himmler) in which SS operatives staged an attack on a German radio station near the Polish border, using it as disinformation to justify the invasion of Poland the following day. This invasion marked the start of World War II. Polish authorities responded with deployments of counterterrorism police, intelligence officers, border guards, and elite units including GROM, NIL, and AGAT; similar warnings were reportedly shared with Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia. Poland foils overnight ‘provocation’ on Kaliningrad border Poland’s intelligence services coordinator, Tomasz Siemoniak, confirmed that authorities assessed a real threat and took preventive measures, while stopping short of endorsing the more specific details of the alleged plot. Those particulars rest on anonymous sources and have not been independently verified. Prime Minister Donald Tusk separately stated that rapid mobilization after suspicious activity near the border – people carrying lights observed near Sępopol who then withdrew – had likely forestalled a provocation, even if the precise intent could not be fully confirmed. The Polish operation coincided with sustained NATO activity in the Baltic region. Warnings that helped prompt the deployments came from Polish services, allied intelligence, and NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich. In the same period, NATO conducted routine air policing intercepts of aircraft traveling to and from Kaliningrad, operated reconnaissance flights (including U.S. Artemis II aircraft) through Polish and Lithuanian airspace near the exclave and the Suwałki Gap, and held exercises involving thousands of troops in Lithuania (Freedom Shield 26-II and Grand Eagle 26) and Poland (including Gallant Cheetah-26). These activities form part of the alliance’s ongoing eastern-flank posture around a strategically sensitive area. Taken together, the episode illustrates a successful instance of early detection and coordinated response that appears to have disrupted a potentially dangerous provocation before it could unfold. The combination of specific intelligence warnings, rapid national deployment of specialized units, and continuous NATO presence and exercises demonstrated readiness without any indication of offensive intent. The episode also shows that NATO’s posture in the region remains oriented toward deterrence: it signals that attempts to test or undermine alliance territory will be identified and met promptly, while underscoring that the alliance seeks to prevent conflict rather than initiate one. In an environment of persistent hybrid threats, such visible, measured responses serve both to protect members and to discourage further adventurism against NATO territory. CIA Director warned Russia against attacking NATO in surprise Moscow visit Caption: The Gleiwitz false-flag op started World War II. Hitler salutes his troops marching in Warsaw. [Photo: public domain]

noticias.titulo: When Russian drones overfly Moldova’s capital
noticias.resumen: Several Russian drones violated Moldova’s airspace on the afternoon and evening of 17 November, with ...
noticias.texto: Several Russian drones violated Moldova’s airspace on the afternoon and evening of 17 November, with one flying directly over the capital Chișinău and prompting President Maia Sandu to denounce the Russian airspace violation. A Gerbera-2 drone has been seen flying directly over Chișinău, the capital of Moldova. pic.twitter.com/9zbqhjdB7p — Faytuks Network (@FaytuksNetwork) November 17, 2026 Moldova’s Defence Ministry reported that seven drones entered the country’s airspace over roughly two and a half hours, five of them crashing near populated areas including sites close to Chișinău; no casualties were reported. President Sandu addressed the public on the social network X , writing that several Russian drones had violated Moldovan airspace, one of them over Chișinău, causing alarm. “Russia’s war threatens all of Europe. Moldova stands on the side of peace. We will continue to push for sanctions against Moscow, support Ukraine, and strengthen our defense capabilities with the help of our partners,” she stated. In further comments she noted that Moldova still lacks the defensive means to protect itself adequately from such drones and therefore must continue condemning the war, backing Ukraine, and investing in national defense with partners. She also accused Moscow of cynicism, observing that while Russian propaganda claims concern for Moldova’s fate, the country sends drones that endanger its citizens’ homes. According to a recent BILD article, Russia has floated transforming Moldova into a federal state comprising the territory controlled by Chișinău, Transnistria and Gagauzia. If Moldova joined the EU, the two pro-Russian regions would gain the right to hold independence referendums. The incidents unfolded against the backdrop of a large-scale Russian aerial assault on Ukraine. According to the Ministry of Defence, the first drone, identified as a Geran-2, entered Moldovan airspace at 15:49 from the direction of Ukraine’s Odesa region and headed toward Tiraspol in the breakaway Transnistria region. Subsequent drones followed. Preliminary data indicated impacts near Cheltuitori in the Chișinău municipality, Pohorniceni and Pogrebeni in Orhei district, Cuhureștii de Jos in Florești district, and Băxani in Soroca district. A sixth impact was reported in Ocnița district, while another aerial vehicle disappeared from monitoring systems near Leova. Fragments recovered in a forest near Naslavcea, roughly 50 meters from the Ukrainian border, were examined by police explosives specialists and identified as belonging to a Gerbera 2-type drone. Operations at six northern border crossing points were temporarily suspended. For security reasons the authorities restricted the entire national airspace at 16:27 after a Shahed-type drone was detected moving from the south toward the Botanica district of Chișinău. The restriction forced an aircraft approaching from Egypt to hold for approximately half an hour in a safe zone before resuming its approach. Moldova’s Air Operations Centre continued monitoring in coordination with relevant institutions and external partners. The designated Ambassador of the Russian Federation to Chișinău, Oleg Ozerov, was summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for 10:00 on 18 November. Russia has consistently rejected Moldova’s accusations of airspace violations, asserting that no proof has been provided that the drones are Russian and accusing Chișinău of inflaming anti-Russian sentiment. Sandu has refused to accept Ozerov’s credentials since his arrival in October 2024. Romania’s ambassador to Moldova, Cristian-Leon Țurcanu, publicly condemned the repeated violations, stating that the incidents of November 17 can no longer be treated as isolated and constitute a direct threat to the population and regional security. “No citizen should have to live under the threat of Russian drones. No one should have to fear for their own safety in their own home, on their own street, or in their own city,” he said. He affirmed Romania’s continued support for Moldova’s independence, territorial integrity, and security, and pledged ongoing assistance in strengthening defence capabilities and protecting civilian infrastructure. “Sovereignty is not negotiable. The security of citizens is not optional. The Republic of Moldova is not alone,” the ambassador declared. Repeated incursions and Moldova’s neutral status Moldova, a small neutral country bordering Ukraine, has faced repeated drone incursions since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Its pro-European government under President Sandu has consistently denounced the war and complained about Russian drones, particularly near the Ukrainian border. Yet drones had rarely approached the capital itself, making the 17 November overflight especially significant. Chișinău lies well inland from the main conflict zones, and the appearance of a drone above residential districts such as Botanica underscored the expanding geographic reach of the fighting. The country’s limited air-defence capabilities leave it heavily reliant on partners. Moldova has sought closer security cooperation with Romania, the European Union, and other Western states while pursuing EU membership by 2030. Transnistria, the Russian-backed separatist region along the Ukrainian border, further complicates the security picture. Political analyst Vitalie Andrievschi observed that authorities are unlikely to escalate beyond formal diplomatic protest. Expelling the Russian ambassador remains improbable under present circumstances. These latest violations occur at a moment when Russia continues intensive long-range strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. Moldova’s experience shows that formal neutrality offers no protection from Russian pressure – and may in fact increase vulnerability to it. Significantly, President Sandu’s government has framed the incidents not merely as technical airspace breaches but as evidence that Russia’s campaign endangers the broader European security order. Sources: Nordnews , Moldpres, Reuters Moscow would like to use Moldova to strike Ukraine, Sandu says Caption: Moldovan police have identified the drone fragments found in a forest near Naslavcea village in Ocnița district as belonging to a Gerbera-2 UAV.
